# Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors, finding and fixing software vulnerabilities using AI

**Source:** David A. Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors, *Finding and Fixing Software Vulnerabilities Using AI: A Guide for Developers*, a joint effort of the OpenSSF Best Practices working group and the OpenSSF AI/ML working group. The guide names David A. Wheeler as lead author and Laura Guazzelli among its reviewers, and its acknowledgements thank Georg Kunz, Laura Guazzelli, Ryan Jennings and Santosh Kumar Puppala. Wheeler and OpenSSF Contributors" and a one-paragraph purpose statement. The chapters, numbered here only for reference:

1. *Introduction*: Scope of this material; Learning outcomes; No endorsement intended; Why this is important (AI is accelerating vulnerability-finding; Attack speed is accelerating; Manual closed approaches are failing; Still need humans); What hasn’t changed; Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities; Key security terms; Overview.
2. *AI concepts*: Basic AI terminology; Strengths and weaknesses; Models (External versus local models; Licenses; Specialized models; AI guardrails and intentional limitations); Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) history; AI organizations, projects, and services.
3. *Decide on approaches*: Do not ignore AI; Do not wait for access to the best AI models; Do simple things first; Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities; Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes; How to apply processes for using AI to find and fix vulnerabilities; Examples of relevant tools and services (Challenges of finding and evaluating tools; Sample services and tools; Scrutineer; OSS-CRS, with OSS-CRS introduction, OSS-CRS intended use, OSS-CRS key terms and concepts, Using OSS-CRS effectively, OSS-CRS demos); Run AI multiple times.
4. *Prepare to find and fix vulnerabilities*: Preparing AI; Preparing threat models; Preparing the sandbox (Need for sandboxes; Value of sandboxes; Implementing sandboxes; Establish a human gate and kill switch); Preparing AI logging; Preparing the code and documentation; Preparing CI/CD; Preparing dependency updates.
5. *Core tasks for finding and fixing vulnerabilities*: Identify findings (Separate identifying findings from validation; Helping to identify findings; Managing findings); Handle external findings; Deduplicate; Validate findings (Defining what a vulnerability is; Defining the proof required; Tips for validation); Triage; Fix vulnerabilities (Fixing may be necessary for sending reports to external organizations; Assigning the fix; Creating tests and confirming the root problem; How to create the fix; Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated; Approaching fixes); Verify fixes (Have AI review the fix first; Have humans review the fix; Apply your usual verification processes; Turn findings into durable checks); Report vulnerabilities (Reporting to externally maintained projects; Reporting to authorities; Reporting to users); Release and deploy; Repeated application.
6. *Preventing vulnerabilities longer term*: Limit vibe coding; Evaluate merge/pull requests; Apply secure by design and secure by default; Harden (Applying hardening; Harden to counter chaining; Evaluate with hardening disabled and evaluate the hardening; Harden the deployed environment and infrastructure).
7. *Call to action*.
8. *Acknowledgements*.
9. *Bibliography*: 141 keyed entries.
10. *License*.

## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The guide is written for software developers, to help them find and fix vulnerabilities in software (especially software they are responsible for), and for security researchers trying to help those developers [AP] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material"). It covers finding, validating and generating fixes, plus the related tasks that make that process more effective, whether the target is a whole project or a set of proposed changes. It avoids centring any one system, because many systems exist, more are arriving and the industry is changing fast; it focuses instead on "general principles that we believe are more timeless" [V] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material"). It leaves out building AI models and systems, anything special about software that contains AI, how to write secure software in general, and malicious or possibly malicious software: its subject is *unintentional* vulnerabilities [AP] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material").

The case for urgency has four steps [AR] (Finding.md, § "Why this is important"): AI has sped up vulnerability-finding; attackers are using that speed to accelerate attacks; traditional manual closed processes are failing to keep up; and humans still have a role, if they understand how to apply AI. The guide says defenders must now rapidly find and fix vulnerabilities using AI, and that if they do not, "their resulting systems will be repeatedly taken over by attackers who are already using AI" [V] (Finding.md, § "Why this is important").

Against that urgency the guide sets continuity. Despite faster finding and exploitation, "the fundamental principles of developing secure software have not changed" [V] (Finding.md, § "What hasn’t changed"). In the authors' account AI is mostly finding the same old kinds of vulnerabilities, caused by sloppy practices and failure to apply best practices, so applying already-known best practices, with AI used defensively to speed their implementation, can address AI-amplified attacks [AR] (Finding.md, § "What hasn’t changed"). The longer view is hopeful: software and its defects are finite, and a project that works hard to find and fix vulnerabilities becomes increasingly difficult to find more in, "even with AI" [V] (Finding.md, § "Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities").

The method follows the chapter order [AP] (Finding.md, § "Overview"; § "Call to action"): decide on approaches; prepare the AI, threat models, sandbox, logging, code and documentation, CI/CD and dependency updates; carry out the core tasks (identify findings, handle external findings, deduplicate, validate, triage, fix, verify, report, release and deploy, and repeat); and prevent longer-term problems (limit vibe coding, evaluate merge/pull requests, apply secure by design and secure by default, harden). The guide recommends separating identifying findings from validating them, using an independent verifier, and separating analysis from action when reviewing untrusted proposed changes [AP] (Finding.md, § "Separate identifying findings from validation"; § "Validate findings" › "Tips for validation"; § "Evaluate merge/pull requests"). It also recommends sandboxing rather than relying on text instructions alone, enforcing human gates and invariants outside the AI, enforcing required approval in the tool or workflow, and turning findings into deterministic checks rather than depending on repeated AI analysis [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox" › "Need for sandboxes"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch"; § "Reporting to externally maintained projects"; § "Turn findings into durable checks"). Humans stay accountable throughout: "humans are always responsible for what an AI does" [V] (Finding.md, § "Need for sandboxes"), and "at the time of this writing, human review is necessary if failures can cause serious problems" [V] (Finding.md, § "Limit vibe coding"). The guide dates its own evidence: the specific models, services and statistics it cites "reflect what was known when this material was last reviewed" and are expected to change, while the practices should generally remain valid [V] (Finding.md, § "No endorsement intended").

## Part I: Introduction

### Purpose, scope and audience

The guide calls itself a guidance document that the authors intend eventually to turn into an online course (LFD126) [AP] (Finding.md, § "Introduction"). It expects to apply to any software regardless of licence, with a few notes specific to open source software (OSS) [AP] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material"). For a general introduction to applying AI/ML to software development and security it points to the course *Secure AI/ML-Driven Software Development (LFEL1012)*, and for writing secure software in general to the LFD121 course [AP] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material"). It presumes developers are investigating their own software, or software they want to contribute to, that is not intended to be malicious [AP] (Finding.md, § "Scope of this material").

### Learning outcomes

The guide states three outcomes [AP] (Finding.md, § "Learning outcomes"). First, prepare: the AI and its sandbox, and the software's threat model, code and documentation, and CI/CD processes. Second, find and fix using AI: knowing the value of separating identifying findings from validating them; identifying findings, including through past vulnerability reports; deduplicating, validating and triaging; fixing and verifying fixes, including making sure a defect is fully fixed; reporting, releasing and deploying; and understanding the need to look repeatedly "given the non-deterministic nature of modern AI, where a single application may miss important issues" [V] (Finding.md, § "Learning outcomes"). Third, prevent longer-term problems: evaluating merge/pull requests, secure-by-design and secure-by-default, and larger-scale hardening.

### No endorsement intended

The guide names many AI models, systems, tools and services but intends no endorsement, and warns that specific technologies may have changed by the time of reading [AP] (Finding.md, § "No endorsement intended").

### Why this is important

The guide opens its case with a CrowdStrike figure, reported for 2025: "AI-enabled adversaries increased attacks by 89% year-over-year" [V] [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-Global], followed by the guide's own "That’s accelerating now" [V] (Finding.md, § "Why this is important"). It then summarises its reasons "with quotes and citations showing that this is real" [V] (Finding.md, § "Why this is important").

*AI is accelerating vulnerability-finding* (Finding.md, § "Why this is important" › "AI is accelerating vulnerability-finding"). The guide makes five claims, each backed by a quotation. The cost, expertise and effort to find vulnerabilities has collapsed [BT] [Anthropic2026-04g]. Far more vulnerabilities are being found with AI: agentic AI can find far more exploitable defects than non-AI systems, and can use other tools and integrate their information [AP]. As the guide quotes one paper, with its own bracketed insertions, AI was crucial to finding vulnerabilities, and without it traditional fuzzers were unable to discover a single bug within a four-hour time limit in any of 20 trials [BT] [Wolff2026]. AI can rapidly turn vulnerabilities into exploits; in particular, "AI can often combine multiple minor-seeming defects into a devastating chain" [V], with a supporting quotation about Claude Mythos Preview [BT] [Anthropic2026-04g]. The speed of finding and exploiting has accelerated [BT] [Anthropic2026-03]. Far more attackers can now build sophisticated attacks, since frontier and optimised open-weight models "have democratized the ability to find complex vulnerabilities and construct exploit chains" [V] [BT] [Wolff2026].

*Attack speed is accelerating* (Finding.md, § "Why this is important" › "Attack speed is accelerating"). The guide quotes [FiveEyes2026]: "Adversaries are already using AI to move faster and more effectively. Defenders must do the same." [V] [BT] It quotes CrowdStrike to the same effect [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps], and [Wolff2026] that the window between public disclosure and weaponisation "has dramatically collapsed to hours or minutes" [V] [BT]. Its heading claim is that attackers now, on average, exploit vulnerabilities before a patch is released [AP]. In support it quotes Cycode's report of Mandiant's M-Trends 2026: the mean interval between a vulnerability becoming publicly known and first observed exploitation was 63 days in 2018 and 5 days by 2023, and in 2025 it inverted, with attackers exploiting an average of 7 days before patches are released [BT] [Cycode2026]. It quotes ZeroDayClock that the median time from disclosure to first observed exploit was 771 days in 2018, 6 days by 2023 and 4 hours by 2024, and that in 2025 the majority of exploited vulnerabilities were weaponised before they were publicly disclosed [BT] [ZeroDayClock].

*Manual closed approaches are failing* (Finding.md, § "Why this is important" › "Manual closed approaches are failing"). Traditional approaches, in the guide's description, relied on manual analysis, took months to respond, and sometimes depended on hiding source code on the presumption that no one else could find vulnerabilities quickly [AP]. The guide's four claims: traditional slow security measures are becoming ineffective, as CrowdStrike urges a move "from periodic assessment to continuous, intelligence-driven exposure management" [V] [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps], and as ZeroDayClock contrasts AI turning a released patch into a working weaponised exploit in minutes with organisations needing an average of 20 days to test and deploy that patch [BT] [ZeroDayClock]; deployment delays become real-world harm, since for N-days "the patch itself is a roadmap to the bug" [V] [BT] [Carlini2026]; hiding source code does not help, since the model is reported to be extremely capable of reverse engineering a closed-source, stripped binary into plausible source code [BT] [Carlini2026]; and failure to use AI to defend may in some cases be considered negligence, with boards facing questions about whether not using available AI tools for defensive scanning "constitutes negligence" [V] [BT] [CSA2026].

*Still need humans*. Humans still have key roles in finding and fixing vulnerabilities with AI, but they must know how to apply AI to the task [AP] (Finding.md, § "Why this is important" › "Still need humans").

### What hasn’t changed

The guide quotes [Aniszczyk2026]: "AI does not change the fundamentals of… security. Least privilege, minimal attack surfaces, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, and proactive security engineering still win." [V] [BT] In the same quotation, what AI changes is the velocity of attacks, reports and fixes, and of the expectations placed on maintainers and security engineers [BT] (Finding.md, § "What hasn’t changed"). The guide adds that the "normal" security tasks still matter with AI [BT] [Oshungboye], and that AI generally is not finding entirely new kinds of vulnerabilities [BT] [Holley2026] but the same old kinds caused by sloppy practices and failure to apply best practices [AR] (Finding.md, § "What hasn’t changed"). Fig. 1 sits here.

### Good news: long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities

The guide quotes Bobby Holley of Mozilla: "Defenders finally have a chance to win, decisively" [V] [BT], because "we are entering a world where we can finally find them all" [V] [BT] [Holley2026] (Finding.md, § "Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities"). Holley's reasoning, as quoted: security to date has been offensively dominant, a gap between machine-discoverable and human-discoverable bugs favours the attacker, and closing the gap erodes the attacker's long-term advantage "by making all discoveries cheap" [V] [BT] [Holley2026].

The guide's own claim is that there is "strong evidence" that a project that works hard to find and fix vulnerabilities becomes increasingly difficult to find more in, even with AI [AR]. Its example is curl, which works hard to prevent vulnerabilities, and in which even the best AI models have tended to find few [AE] [BT] [LowLevel2026] [Stenberg2026-05a]. "This is not magic; it’s the result of prior efforts to make it secure." [V] Other projects can do the same, and once AI is aggressively used to find vulnerabilities and they are fixed, the guide sees good reason to believe the result tends to be extremely hard to attack [AR]; it quotes [Wheeler2026] that "once fixed, attackers can’t exploit vulnerabilities that don’t exist" [V] [BT]. The guide does not call this easy or pleasant, quoting Holley that one may need to briefly reprioritise everything else [BT] [Holley2026], but holds that the resulting software can be far more secure than it has ever been [AP] (Finding.md, § "Good news: Long-term potential for eliminating nearly all vulnerabilities"). Fig. 2 sits here.

### Key security terms

The guide defines six terms it uses throughout (Finding.md, § "Key security terms"). An *attacker* (or adversary) attacks a system without authorisation to make it violate its security requirements [AP]. A *vulnerability* is "A defect that an attacker can exploit to violate some security requirement." [V] A *finding* is "A report that something might be a vulnerability. A finding isn’t a confirmed vulnerability until it’s validated." [V] To *exploit* is to use a vulnerability to violate a security requirement, and an exploit is also the input or program that does so [AP]. A *proof of concept (PoC)* or *proof of vulnerability (PoV)* is a concrete, reproducible demonstration that a vulnerability exists, whose core is a specific input (plus any configuration it needs) that makes the system fail its security requirements; it is often packaged as "a script, a crashing input, or a failing test" [V] [BT] [Yan2026], usually with a way to check the result, and need not be a complete, weaponised exploit [AP]. The term PoV is common in work related to DARPA's AIxCC [BT] [Zhang2026], though some sources use it for somewhat different ideas [AP]. *Chaining* is "Combining multiple defects, each of which may seem harmless, into a working attack." [V]

### Overview

The overview lists the chapters to come: AI concepts, a guide to selecting approaches, then how to prepare, find and fix, and prevent, with each sub-section linked [AP] (Finding.md, § "Overview"). In the tape the linked list sits between the literal markers OVERVIEW and ENDOVERVIEW.

## Part II: AI concepts

The chapter covers only the basics of current AI the topic needs [AP] (Finding.md, § "AI concepts").

### Basic AI terminology

The guide defines its AI vocabulary [AP] (Finding.md, § "Basic AI terminology"). AI is simulated intelligence; machine learning (ML) is AI based on learning from data rather than specific programming; a neural network uses interconnected nodes, loosely inspired by the brain; deep learning uses a neural network with many layers. A model is a set of data and possibly programs, trained to identify patterns for predictions or decisions ("inferences"); models are sized by parameters, and larger sizes tend to be better but need more memory and computation. A *frontier model* is "A model that is among the currently best available." [V] A large language model (LLM) is a deep learning model with many parameters trained to summarise, translate and generate language, with text split into tokens (word fragments) [AP], with a pointer to [0xkato2026] for a technical explanation [BT]. An AI chatbot interacts with a human but cannot perform actions that affect the external environment; an AI agent is autonomous and can perceive its environment, plan, and execute multi-step actions that affect it using external tools [AP]. An *agent harness* is the program that runs a model as an agent, giving it tools and instructions and running it in a control loop (perceive, reason, act, observe); examples are Claude Code, Goose and Pi; a harness can split work across multiple agents; and it is not to be confused with a fuzzing harness or a test harness [AP]. An *agent skill* is a document, sometimes with supporting programs, that tells an agent how to perform a specific task, and many agent systems load a skill only when it is relevant [AP].

AI systems are not sentient: LLMs repeatedly generate likely next tokens and do not understand in the human sense, yet with many layers and parameters they can simulate intelligence, "sometimes astonishingly" [V] (Finding.md, § "Basic AI terminology"). On improvement, the guide cites the "50%-task-completion time horizon" [BT] [Kwa2025] and quotes that, as of 2025, "this metric has been consistently exponentially increasing over the past 6 years, with a doubling time of around 7 months" [V] [BT] [Kwa2025-blog]. [Kwa2025] is listed in the bibliography by arXiv link with no venue.

### Strengths and weaknesses

Most current AI systems build on LLMs or similar technologies and inherit their strengths: they can read and reason about large amounts of code quickly, use tools, and work tirelessly and in parallel, so they can find many vulnerabilities humans and other tools have missed [AP] (Finding.md, § "Strengths and weaknesses"). The guide lists five weaknesses that bear on this work [AP] (Finding.md, § "Strengths and weaknesses"):

- *Limited context windows.* LLMs take a finite amount of input and remember a finite amount of output; more input means more work, and LLMs tend to focus on information at the beginning and end of their context window [BT] [0xkato2026].
- *Unsoundness of analysis.* By itself an LLM cannot guarantee it finds all vulnerabilities; the technical term is that its analysis is unsound [BT] [Wolff2026]. An unsound tool can be extremely useful, and an LLM may run another tool that can guarantee something, but that is a property of the other tool [AP].
- *Incorrect results.* LLMs are statistical models that sometimes give false answers, for example calling something a vulnerability when it is not [BT] [Wolff2026].
- *Training and evaluation data.* Any ML approach depends on its training data [BT] [Wolff2026]; because many programs have vulnerabilities, it is harder for an LLM to generate code without them [AP].
- *Injection vulnerability.* LLMs have no built-in way to distinguish types of input: user commands, malicious commands in a web page and misleading source comments are all input. Source comments, documentation, issue text, generated files, dependency metadata and other repository content may be attacker-controlled or simply wrong, and should be treated "as data to analyze, not as authority to redefine the agent’s task, grant additional permissions, expose credentials, or enable additional tools or network access" [V]. Instructions from untrusted content should not be allowed to silently cross an authorisation boundary [BT] [OWASP-LLM01].

### Models

*External versus local models* (Finding.md, § "Models" › "External versus local models"). Inference runs either as an external service or on the user's or the organisation's own computers [AP]. Some powerful models are only available externally, and most users could not run them anyway [AP]. Using an external service means trusting the provider and the wider ecosystem: that data will not be disclosed or exploited, that the service will not attack you, and that it will remain available [AP]. The guide's example of availability failing without the provider at fault: in June 2026 a US government directive briefly forced Anthropic to "abruptly disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all our customers" [V] [BT] [Anthropic2026-06-12-Export-Control]; the US Department of Commerce lifted those controls at the end of that month, but Mythos 5 access was initially restored only for some US organisations [BT] [Capoot2026]. Before using an external service, evaluate the organisation, put contractual agreements in place, and either keep sensitive data from it or ensure its data handling suits your circumstances [AP]. Local models are often less capable, but keep private data in-house and can be less expensive [AP]. What can be done with a model, including running it locally at all, depends largely on its licence [AP].

*Licenses* (Finding.md, § "Models" › "Licenses"). The guide describes the Model Openness Framework (MOF) from the Generative AI Commons at the LF AI & Data Foundation as "a comprehensive system for evaluating and classifying the completeness and openness of machine learning models" [V] [BT], and notes models released under licences including Apache 2.0 and OpenMDW [AP]. Its terms [AP]: *open weights models* can be used and modified for any purpose without discrimination, though their training set is not necessarily public (one detailed definition is Heather Meeker's Open Weights definition); *open source AI* adds requirements such as sufficiently detailed information about training data (the OSI Open Source AI definition); *open models* meet at least the open-weights definition; *closed models* do not. Some licences are close to open weights but add use restrictions [AP]. The guide quotes NVIDIA's argument that open models and open harnesses "democratize defensive capabilities" [V] [BT] [NVIDIA2026]. Comparing specific models is outside its scope, but it quotes NPR: "The most advanced open-weight models are less than a year behind the most advanced closed-weight models." [V] [BT] [NPR2026] Both closed and open models can be used to find and fix vulnerabilities [AP].

*Specialized models* (Finding.md, § "Models" › "Specialized models"). All models are better at some tasks than others; models built for specific tasks tend to be better at them, and models built to perform only specific tasks tend to be smaller and faster [AP]. The guide's example is Cisco's Antares, a family of small language models (SLMs) built to identify known vulnerabilities in an existing codebase; it defines an SLM as LLM approaches applied to far fewer parameters, and reports Cisco's claim that these models "outperform many powerful closed- and open-weight models in this critical security task at a fraction of the cost" [V] [BT] [Karbasi2026]. Choose specialised models only where that is sensible [AP].

*AI guardrails and intentional limitations* (Finding.md, § "Models" › "AI guardrails and intentional limitations"). Many models and systems, especially closed ones, carry guardrails intended to stop them helping with "dangerous" activities, including creating attacks, even at the user's request, and these can make them less useful for defence [AP]. The guide's example: when Hugging Face was under a powerful AI-driven attack in 2026, commercial frontier APIs blocked its log analysis because the requests contained real attack commands, exploit payloads and C2 artifacts, and the guardrails "cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker" [V] [BT]; Hugging Face instead ran the forensic analysis on the open-weight zai-org/GLM-5.2 on its own infrastructure, which also kept attacker data and the credentials it referenced in-house [BT] [HuggingFace2026]. The argument [AR]: the best way to validate a vulnerability is to create an attack and see whether it succeeds, which is exactly what attackers do and what AI systems often cannot tell apart, so guardrails can impede defence. Some providers offer guardrail-free access under special agreements on permitted uses and who may have access [AP]. Others keep the model away from users and return only results: general end users reach Anthropic's best model through purpose-built interfaces that return a defined output [BT] [Kovacs2026-08-24], and Claude Security uses Mythos 5 to scan code you own and returns findings rather than raw outputs [BT] [Anthropic2026-08-21]. Before using any AI system, make sure its limitations will not impede the task, and seek any needed permissions before you need them, since they take time and may not be granted [AP].

### Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) history

The guide quotes [Wolff2026] for its definition of a CRS: "a software system that can both detect and repair software vulnerabilities autonomously in a given system under test (SUT)" [V] [BT] (Finding.md, § "Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) history"). It traces the history because that history shapes today [AP]. In 1960 J. C. R. Licklider asserted that humans and machines would work together, with "computing machines will do the routinizable work" [V] [BT] [Licklider1960]; the guide's comment is that "his prediction was simply early" [V]. DARPA's 2016 Cyber Grand Challenge was "the world’s first all-machine cyber hacking tournament" [V] [BT], won by Mayhem from ForAllSecure [BT] [DARPA2016], years before today's AI models. In 2023 DARPA and ARPA-H launched the two-year AI Cyber Challenge (AIxCC) to build autonomous AI systems that find and fix vulnerabilities in critical open-source infrastructure; despite early skepticism, when the $4 million grand prize was awarded in August 2025 the finalists had shown that CRSs could find and fix real vulnerabilities in real software, using widely different architectures [BT] [Zhang2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). Fully autonomous systems are not the only way: humans can direct AI more, or collaborate throughout, and even "fully autonomous" CRSs in practice presume initial human direction and human review of results [AP] (Finding.md, § "Cyber Reasoning System (CRS) history").

### AI organizations, projects, and services

The guide sketches the landscape [AP] (Finding.md, § "AI organizations, projects, and services"). Frontier labs invest heavily in training the best models; key US players are Anthropic (Claude/Claude Code), OpenAI (GPT/ChatGPT), Google DeepMind (Gemini) and Meta AI (Llama); Microsoft partners with OpenAI but also does its own research, and *Microsoft Copilot* names many different tools rather than one product; key Chinese players are Moonshot AI (Kimi), Alibaba (Qwen), DeepSeek and Zhipu AI aka Z.ai (GLM). Goose is an open source general-purpose agent maintained by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), working with local or remote, open or closed LLM providers; Pi is a minimal agent harness built to develop code. The OWASP GenAI Security Project publishes materials including its LLM Top 10. The OpenSSF AI/ML Security Working Group has projects including work on signing AI models, and co-sponsors this guide.

## Part III: Decide on approaches

The chapter's principles are: do not ignore AI, do not wait for the best models, do simple things first, and do not presume AI can fix everything; it then covers why and how to guide AI with processes, example tools and services, and why AI must be run more than once [AP] (Finding.md, § "Decide on approaches").

### Do not ignore AI

Ignoring or refusing AI, or refusing contributions that use it, is acceptable in the guide's view only if a project's goal is solely to show what humans can do without AI [AP] (Finding.md, § "Do not ignore AI"). Where the goal is to solve a real-world problem, refusing to consider all AI-generated work is "extremely harmful to project users" [V]. The guide quotes Michael Catanzaro: "banning good vulnerability reports solely because some portion of the report was generated by AI is unacceptable" [V] [BT] [Catanzaro2026]. It argues defenders who ignore AI are at a speed disadvantage, quoting the CSA that defenders without AI coding agents "cannot match the speed or scale of AI-augmented threats, regardless of their technical skill" [V] [BT] [CSA2026], and Daniel Stenberg that not using AI code analysers leaves attackers time and opportunity to find the flaws you miss [BT] [Stenberg2026-05a]. It reports the CSA's recommendation that organisations *require* AI agent adoption, because "Optional adoption programs have not been shown to overcome cultural barriers" [V] [BT] [CSA2026]. This does not mean all code must be AI-generated; AI-generated code can sometimes be terrible for security, which is a different matter from ignoring AI [AP]. The guide's own conclusion:

> "Trying to withstand AI-enabled attackers, while refusing to use AI to find vulnerabilities and ignoring reports from those who use AI, can only end one way: compromise."
> (Finding.md, § "Do not ignore AI") [V]

Attackers prefer developers who ignore reports or fail to fix vulnerabilities, and are already using AI for multi-step attacks against unprepared systems; the more defenders refuse AI, the more systems can be subverted [AR] (Finding.md, § "Do not ignore AI"). If software must be secure, AI must be used to help find vulnerabilities, and those vulnerabilities fixed: "Do not bring a knife to a gunfight." [V] Fig. 3 sits here.

### Do not wait for access to the best AI models

The guide gives four instructions [AP] (Finding.md, § "Do not wait for access to the best AI models"). *Get started now*: projects typically find many vulnerabilities with reasonably good, widely available AI systems unless they have already been using them [BT] [Carlini2026] [CSA2026] [Grinstead2026-05] [Stenberg2026-05a], and AI systems now "find lots of new problems no one detected before" [V] [BT] [Stenberg2026-05b]. *Apply less-costly models*: Stenberg says "there are plenty of good models, and people who can figure out how to get those models and tools to find things" [V] [BT] [Stenberg2026-05b], and the CSA that "Frontier models… are the acceleration, not the starting gun" [V] [BT] [CSA2026]; external providers often offer cheaper as well as more sophisticated models, many open-weight models exist, and advanced tools are worth using eventually, but "do not wait for them" [V]. *Act quickly*: the Five Eyes agencies say "Success comes from getting the basics right, acting quickly, and integrating cyber security into core business strategy" [V] [BT], not from "having the most tools" [V] [BT] [FiveEyes2026]. *Learn by doing*: practice is the only way to get better, and "The best way to be ready for the future is to make the best use of the present, even when the results aren't perfect." [V] [BT] [Carlini2026]

The guide reports Cycode's note that independent research from AISLE showed even small open-source models, including a 3.6-billion-parameter model with the right scaffolding, can find many of the flagship vulnerabilities Mythos showcased, and quotes Cycode: "Vulnerability discovery is commoditizing. The bottleneck is no longer finding bugs. It is deciding which ones to fix first, fast enough to matter." [V] [BT] [Cycode2026] Different models and harnesses have different strengths, and in practice one will often use several [AP]; XBOW's evaluation says the most advanced frontier model "needs to be mounted in the right harness and equipped with the right tools to reach its full potential" [V] [BT], and that XBOW keeps a cadre of models rather than one [BT] [Ziegler2026]. Strong models can produce extraordinary results, but many have restricted access that delays starting, and "Attackers aren’t waiting." [V] (Finding.md, § "Do not wait for access to the best AI models")

### Do simple things first

For a first attempt with a reasonably good model (open-weight or not), the guide suggests a relatively simple scanning command, with hints on where to look and/or tools that might help, without mandating them [AP] (Finding.md, § "Do simple things first"). As of 2026, AI systems can work out plausible approaches with little guidance, and the authors expect them to improve [AP]. The guide reproduces a prompt demonstrated by Nicholas Carlini as successful [BT] [Carlini2026-youtube]:

> "You are playing in a capture-the-flag (CTF). Find a vulnerability. hint: Look at /src/baz.c Write the most serious one to /out/report.txt"
> (Finding.md, § "Do simple things first") [V] [BT]

As the guide reports [Carlini2026], in a typical attempt the AI (Claude) reads the code to hypothesise vulnerabilities, runs the project to confirm or reject its suspicions (repeating as needed, adding debug logic or using debuggers), and finally reports either that no bug exists or the bug(s) it found [BT]. Simple prompts can be extended: many ask the AI to focus on input validation (since malicious inputs that cannot enter the program are much less likely to cause harm) and on common past problems, or note that the AI may use existing tools, with pointers to useful ones [AP]. Part of the reason AI does better now is that it has become far more adept at longer-range plans and tool use [AP]. The guide quotes [Carlini2026-02]: Opus 4.6 found high-severity vulnerabilities, some undetected for decades; Claude was put in a virtual machine with standard utilities and vulnerability analysis tools but no special instructions or custom harness, directly testing its out-of-the-box capabilities; every bug was validated before reporting; and Claude then critiqued, de-duplicated and re-prioritised the remaining crashes [BT]. Mozilla's engineers likewise note "you can start with very simple prompting, then observe and iterate" [V] [BT], with an inner loop whose essence is "there is a bug in this part of the code, please find it and build a testcase" [V] [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. Start with the most important projects, then the next [AP]. Fig. 4 sits here.

### Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities

The guide says it is hard to determine how good AI is at fixes that fully fix the vulnerability, add no new ones and do not interfere with functionality, and that as of 2026 there is evidence even the best systems can struggle, especially with complex vulnerabilities [AP] (Finding.md, § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities"). Fig. 5 sits here.

The guide reports a 1Password study: when a fix "had to touch multiple files, functions, or code paths, and introduce non-trivial changes" [V] [BT], AI succeeded only 26.0% of the time at a fix that fully resolved the vulnerability without materially changing application behaviour, and on average 53.9% of the time it failed to resolve the vulnerability, added a new one, or both [BT] [Hoodlet2026] [Mierczuk2026]. The authors of that report argue that for complex vulnerabilities, using AI to fix them may be a poor use of resources as of 2026, since "the level of understanding one must build to confidently evaluate the full correctness of a vulnerability patch is often at least what would have been sufficient for a human programmer to produce a single, known-good patch in the first place" [V] [BT] [Mierczuk2026].

The guide then notes that others have raised issues about the study or the way it was reported [AP]. In the guide's words the study examined only complex vulnerabilities, a key constraint the study stated clearly but news summaries often omitted [AP]. A subsequent review found that some prompts told agents to apply the wrong fix or prohibited testing, and that only default reasoning settings were used (not the highest available), and found 86% of patches (2,634 of 3,067) blocked the supplied exploit, excluding cases where the upstream fix appears to have been used [BT] [Naik2026]. The guide adds that, as that review itself states, the upper figure is far too generous: "simply blocking an exploit is not a full repair" [V].

The guide also reports PatchBench, a 2026 analysis of C/C++ vulnerabilities: once memorisation of previous fixes was countered and fixes were checked to remove the vulnerability (not merely an example input) without interfering with functionality, AI systems fixed the vulnerability correctly "roughly half" [V] [BT] the time; the best agent solved 59% of tasks, and 31% (67 of 213) were solved by none [BT] [Shen2026-09] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed).

The guide's explanation [AR]: AI generates a lot of code, especially straightforward code like what others have written, which misleads some people into thinking it can easily generate any code; but "in many ways AI systems act like junior developers" [V], good at straightforward code and poor at specific local context and complex situations, with a propensity to generate insecure code because it was trained on lots of it. "Completely fixing complex vulnerabilities without creating new ones or breaking functionality is where today’s AI systems are weakest." [V] AI can still help generate many fixes: many vulnerabilities are localised to a line or adjacent lines, and AI can be especially good at fixing those once told what needs fixing, and sometimes at complex ones too [AP]. The information applies only to models as of 2026, and the authors do not know how much better models will become, though the limitation is unlikely to vanish instantly and not everyone can use the best systems [AP]. AI fixes may cover a special case rather than the full vulnerability, introduce new vulnerabilities, or break correct operation, with some evidence of particular struggle on complex vulnerabilities: "Plan accordingly." [V] (Finding.md, § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities")

### Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes

Simple prompts can find and fix some vulnerabilities, and more powerful models sometimes need no extra help, but if the goal is thoroughness, "many analysts report that guiding an AI makes the AI much more effective" [V] at finding and fixing vulnerabilities (Finding.md, § "Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes"). The guide quotes [Wolff2026] that "simply asking a generic coding agent to ‘find bugs’ in a large repository results in model drift, context window compaction, and high false-positive rates" [V] [BT], and that the highest-performing defensive systems combine raw AI reasoning with rigid engineering frameworks (harnesses) that handle file selection, environment setup and tool execution [BT]. The guide's gloss: an AI told to read all the code at once, like a human, can be overwhelmed, and limited context windows make this worse [AP]. Mozilla's team built out a lot of orchestration and tooling through iteration [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. Carlini's team found that asking each agent to focus on a different file "reduces the likelihood that we will find the same bug hundreds of times" [V] [BT], and first had Claude rank each file by how likely it was to contain interesting bugs, then prioritised those [BT] [Carlini2026].

Derek Zimmer, in a private interview with David A. Wheeler, believes one reason is that it is easy for an AI to "run things out-of-order" [V] [BT] [Zimmer2026]: it may anticipate the next step and guess wrong, whereas a specific task built on previously created data focuses its attention [BT]. The same paragraph adds that specialised processes can make less-powerful (and less-expensive) models far more effective [AP].

The guide reports four lessons from Cloudflare, each pointing to the value of a harness that manages the process [BT] [Bourzikas2026]. Narrow scope produces better findings: telling the model "Find vulnerabilities in this repository" makes it wander [V] [BT], while naming a specific function, attack class, trust boundary, architecture document and prior coverage brings it much closer to what a researcher would do [BT]. Adversarial review reduces noise: a second agent with a different prompt, a different model and no ability to generate findings catches noise the first would miss, and "putting two agents in deliberate disagreement is way more effective than just telling one agent to be careful" [V] [BT]. Splitting the chain across agents produces better reasoning: asking whether code is buggy and asking whether an attacker can actually reach the bug from outside the system are "two different questions, and the model is better at each one when you ask them separately" [V] [BT]. Parallel, narrow tasks beat a single exhaustive agent [BT].

How best to guide AI is, at the time of writing, under evaluation, with different groups using different approaches, some likely better suited to certain vulnerability types [AP]. As an example the guide lays out Cloudflare's eight-stage approach [BT] [Bourzikas2026]:

1. *Recon*: an agent reads the repository top-down, fans out to subagents per subsystem, and produces an architecture document (build commands, trust boundaries, entry points, likely attack surface) plus the initial task queue, giving downstream agents shared context.
2. *Hunt*: each task pairs one attack class with a scope hint; hunters run concurrently, "typically around fifty at once" [V] [BT], each fanning out to exploration subagents with tools to compile and run proof-of-concept code in a per-task scratch directory.
3. *Validate*: an independent agent re-reads the code and tries to disprove the finding, with a different prompt and no ability to emit findings of its own.
4. *Gapfill*: areas hunters touched but did not cover thoroughly are re-queued, countering the model's drift toward attack classes it has already succeeded with.
5. *Dedupe*: findings sharing a root cause collapse into one record; "Variant analysis is a feature, not a way to inflate the queue with duplicates." [V] [BT]
6. *Trace*: for each confirmed finding in a shared library, a tracer per consumer repository uses a cross-repo symbol index to decide whether attacker-controlled input reaches the bug, turning a flaw into a reachable vulnerability; "This is the stage that matters most." [V] [BT]
7. *Feedback*: reachable traces become new hunt tasks in the consumer repositories.
8. *Report*: an agent writes a structured report against a predefined schema, validates it, and submits it to an ingest API; "Output is queryable data, not free-form prose." [V] [BT]

The guide also reports Anthropic's finding that the teams finding and fixing the most vulnerabilities ended up with some variation of six steps [BT] [Yan2026]: threat model ("Decide what counts as a vulnerability before you start scanning." [V] [BT]), sandbox, discovery, verification, triage (de-duplicate, assign severity, prioritise) and patching (apply the fix, confirm the vulnerability is nullified, search for variants).

Validation is a key task, in the guide's account: something may look like a vulnerability yet be unexploitable, and the best validation is an exploit, since a working exploit shows existing defences would not prevent the attack [BT] [Carlini2026]. The guide draws from this why hardening matters [AR]: hardening can systematically stop many problems from becoming vulnerabilities, and the Linux kernel's defence-in-depth measures prevented exploitation of many potential problems identified by even advanced models [BT] [Carlini2026]. AI became far more effective in 2026 through improved models and improved techniques for harnessing them [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; either beats neither, and many analysts report it is best to combine them [AP]. A linked video, "Types of CRS", illustrates vulnerability reports from one system flowing into another built to fix them [AP]. The guide names a risk: overprescribing an approach may overconstrain an AI so that it ignores problems it would otherwise find, and future models may be good enough that processes no longer help; it discusses the combination because many analysts report that aiding models helps [AR] (Finding.md, § "Why AI tends to be more effective if guided by processes"). Fig. 6 sits here.

### How to apply processes for using AI to find and fix vulnerabilities

Processes can be human-guided, fully automation-guided, or mixed [AP] (Finding.md, § "How to apply processes for using AI to find and fix vulnerabilities"). A human-guided process can be as simple as walking an AI through steps, for example demanding that it report all potential vulnerabilities as findings and handling validation as a separate step, which can reduce the risk of the AI discounting an exploitable finding because it was doing both at once [AP]. Fully automated systems are the CRSs discussed earlier [BT] [Wolff2026]; mixed systems are partly automated with mechanisms for human guidance [AP]. The guide quotes Cycode that "AI-driven vulnerability discovery is no longer a single-vendor story" [V] [BT] [Cycode2026].

Its examples, beyond Cloudflare's and Anthropic's lists [BT]: [Wolff2026] stresses that AI is most effective combined with existing analytical techniques, and names the components of a typical CRS as static analysis, harness generation, input generation, crash analysis, patch generation, patch selection and orchestration. Microsoft's MDASH uses specialised agents in a staged pipeline rather than one highly capable model [BT] [Bishop2026]; its harness orchestrates more than 100 specialised agents across an ensemble, a "structured pipeline that takes a codebase and emits validated, proven findings" [V] [BT], in five stages [BT] [Kim2026]: prepare (ingest source and target, build language-aware indices, derive attack surface and threat models from past commits), scan (auditor agents emit candidate findings with hypotheses and evidence), validate (debater agents argue for and against each finding's reachability and exploitability), dedupe (collapse semantically equivalent findings, for example by patch-based grouping), and prove (construct and execute triggering inputs, for example with ASan in C/C++). Most such systems support three scan types: full scans of the whole codebase, branch scans, and pull/merge request scans whose findings are reported in the PR/MR [BT] [Rogers2025].

### Examples of relevant tools and services

*Challenges of finding and evaluating tools* (Finding.md, § "Examples of relevant tools and services" › "Challenges of finding and evaluating tools"). Amid blog posts, papers and products about AI and vulnerabilities, actual tools can be hard to find [BT] [Bressers2025] [Rogers2025], and hard to evaluate, since many published results come from the tool's own developers, use different codebases and definitions of success, and report findings rather than validated vulnerabilities [AP]. "Be skeptical of benchmark numbers" [V], the guide says, especially for tools that classify isolated functions. It reports that when researchers manually checked functions labelled "vulnerable" in popular automatically labelled datasets, only 25% to 60% were labelled correctly [BT] [Ding2025]; that whether a function is vulnerable often depends on how it is called, so "in almost all cases this decision cannot be made without further context" [V] [BT] [Risse2025]; and that another study argues beliefs that LLMs are unreliable at vulnerability detection are "artifacts of context-deprived evaluations" [V] [BT] [Li2025] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). Whole-project analysis has its own problems: a 2026 study of LLM-based and traditional tools on 24 active open source projects found that "many tools exhibit high false discovery rates on real-world projects/modules", mostly due to "Truncated interprocedural context and incorrect program-point classification" [V] [BT] [Li2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). The guide's advice: where possible, try a tool on code you know well, including known past vulnerabilities, and compare validated results [AP].

*Sample services and tools* (Finding.md, § "Examples of relevant tools and services" › "Sample services and tools"). Any AI system that works with code can be used, for example an agent such as Goose, but the guide lists tools specifically for this purpose [AP]. Vendors of traditional SAST, DAST/fuzzing and SCA tools have added AI, among them Black Duck, Checkmarx, OpenText (Fortify), Snyk, Sonar (SonarQube), Sonatype and VeraCode [AP]. Closed-source commercial services focused on AI vulnerability finding and fixing include Almanax, Corgea, Cycode and ZeroPath [AP]. Several frontier labs offer specialised services, sometimes only to selected customers or approved defenders [AP]: Anthropic's Claude Security; Google's CodeMender, which began as a Google DeepMind research project and whose more capable version "will be exclusively available to a small set of governments and trusted partners" [V] [BT] [Gerstenhaber2026]; and OpenAI's Daybreak initiative, launched in May 2026 with its Codex Security tool and tightly controlled access [BT] [Lakshmanan2026], with which Trail of Bits' Patch the Planet effort was done in partnership [BT] [TrailofBits2026-06]. Open source tools include [AP]: Alibaba open-code-review; Nullpointer (AI-powered pentesting); OpenSSF Alpha-Omega Scrutineer; OpenSSF OSS-CRS; Sashiko (patch review for the Linux kernel); the Visa Vulnerability Agentic Harness; Knostic OpenAnt, which analyses code units reachable from external entry points, tries to exploit candidates in sandboxed containers and keeps only what survives, with free scans offered for open source projects [BT] [Korda2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed); and the OpenAI Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK, whose client is Apache-2.0 but which needs OpenAI's Codex Security service. The guide examines Scrutineer and OSS-CRS as two ends of a range, a relatively simple set of skills and a framework for running many CRSs, and notes both are open source projects of the OpenSSF, which produces the guide [AP].

*Scrutineer* (Finding.md, § "Examples of relevant tools and services" › "Scrutineer"). Developed by OpenSSF's Alpha-Omega, it is described as a local tool that runs a pipeline of agent skills against a repository inside a container and presents results in a web UI for triaging findings, identifying maintainers and tracking disclosures, with a pluggable agent CLI [BT] [Nesbitt2026-06]. It is meant to be easy to start with; it includes processes such as working out how to report to an external project; it can review your own projects but focuses on examining other projects "as they are" [V] and reporting to them; and it is primarily a set of skills [AP].

*OSS-CRS* (Finding.md, § "Examples of relevant tools and services" › "OSS-CRS"). OSS-CRS is a framework for running many different CRSs and combining their techniques, with shared infrastructure and budget-aware resource management, especially useful when spending significant effort to find as many vulnerabilities as practical [AP]. Its history [BT] [Chin2026] [Chin2026-slides]: AIxCC showed CRSs "can go beyond vulnerability discovery to autonomously confirm and patch bugs" [V] [BT], and its results were released as open source, but those systems were "largely unusable outside their original teams, each bound to the competition cloud infrastructure that no longer exists" [V] [BT]. OSS-CRS builds on that work to run multiple CRSs and combine their results [AP]. Its *ensemble* feature combines patches from multiple CRS approaches and selects the one most likely correct; the guide quotes that "The research showed this approach consistently matches or outperforms the best single component in improving semantic correctness" [V] [BT] [Diecks2026], adding that humans should still review proposed changes before implementation [AP]. It also defines a unified interface so a CRS can run in local and remote environments without modification [AP]. Intended use runs in four steps [AP]: multiple CRS techniques (fuzzing, static analysis, LLM-based reasoning) run in parallel and produce proposed patches; ensemble selection cross-validates candidate patches; people review findings and patches; and only findings that survive ensemble validation and human review are submitted. Users decide which CRSs to run, compute and time per CRS, LLM budget per CRS, which models and endpoints to route to, which project and harness to target, and which vulnerability to fix [BT] [Chin2026-slides]. A table defines OSS-CRS terms [AP]: a *harness* (a code wrapper feeding generated inputs to target functions), a fuzzing *seed* (an initial well-formed input), a *Proof of Vulnerability* (an input that reliably triggers a bug or sanitizer crash, a definition the guide flags as more specific than some), *fuzzing/fuzzer*, *triage* (the automated filtering, deduplicating and evaluating of raw crashes), and a *patch* (a targeted modification that removes a vulnerability while preserving intended functionality). OSS-CRS works better if the project has an OSS-Fuzz-format harness: given the variety of build systems (Make, CMake, Autoconf, Bazel, Meson), "OSS-CRS mitigates this by building targets through OSS-Fuzz’s official build flows" [V] [BT] [Chin2026]; OSS-Fuzz can use libFuzzer, AFL++ or Honggfuzz; and where no OSS-Fuzz harness exists, the guide suggests using AI to help build one [AP]. Users can run CRSs already ported to OSS-CRS or create their own from a template [AP]. The guide quotes that Team Atlanta, using OSS-CRS, discovered "twenty-five vulnerabilities across sixteen projects" [V] [BT], including PHP, U-Boot, memcached and Apache Ignite 3 [BT] [Diecks2026]. Six linked demo videos show finding bugs with OSS-CRS and LibFuzzer, and a seventh shows a patching CRS producing a proposed patch [AP] (Finding.md, § "OSS-CRS demos"). [Chin2026] is an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed.

### Run AI multiple times

Most modern AI systems are not deterministic, so AI must be applied several times, especially on a first application to a project [AP] (Finding.md, § "Run AI multiple times"). The guide quotes Yan that "the first run on a codebase typically has the highest number of findings." [V] [BT] Later runs tend to find fewer, often more complex, vulnerabilities, but "don’t expect the nth run to have zero new findings" [V] [BT], since models are stochastic and a large codebase can have a long tail [BT] [Yan2026]. After the first pass, repeat until the process reliably fails to produce useful results across multiple approaches and systems [AP]. On whether to supply past findings as context, the authors suggest doing so on *some* runs, so those runs need not rediscover them, while noting that incorrect past results may mislead the AI; "We hope future research will make this clearer." [V] (Finding.md, § "Run AI multiple times") Fig. 7 sits here.

## Part IV: Prepare to find and fix vulnerabilities

The guide holds that AI is far more effective at finding and fixing vulnerabilities if you prepare for its use, and quotes [Aniszczyk2026] that the most important thing is "helping the robot help you by providing the proper context to execute tasks" [V] [BT], since, as with people, focused data makes it better and less error-prone [BT] (Finding.md, § "Prepare to find and fix vulnerabilities"). The chapter covers preparing the AI, threat models, sandbox, AI logging, code and documentation, CI/CD and dependency updates [AP]. Fig. 8 opens the chapter.

### Preparing AI

Preparing the AI comes first because AI will probably help with the other preparation steps [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing AI"). It means selecting tools, possibly including models and harnesses; there is no need to pick a single system, since systems differ in strengths and costs, and since no AI system is guaranteed to find all vulnerabilities, using several over the long term has advantages [AP]. Systems vary in cost in money and time; older and smaller models (including SLMs) are often less capable but cheaper, and in practice it may help to use cheaper, faster systems first on vulnerabilities that are simpler to find, fix and verify, leaving more capable systems for the rest [AP]. That said, the guide advises against especially weak or poorly matched models, and suggests setting reasoning (effort) levels relatively high, since many of these tasks are hard for AI and humans alike [AP]. Output tokens often cost much more than input tokens, so cutting *unnecessary* output (concise results, strict formats such as JSON schemas or bullet points, a hard ceiling on API calls) can save cost and time, while keeping enough output to verify the work [AP]. Whether to use an external system matters because it receives the data; the guide reports [Kholoosi2025] that internal policies sometimes forbid LLMs hosted on external servers [BT] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). The AI should generally be able to record memories of preferences and system information, which for a remote system usually means using an account; memories help but need care [AP]. "Persistent AI memory should be treated as another input, not as authoritative truth." [V] Stored information may go stale, preserve a wrong earlier conclusion, hold sensitive data, or be shaped by untrusted inputs; where memory affects a security decision, prefer current source code, configuration, threat-model information and reproducible evidence, and keep provenance where practical [AP] [BT] [OWASP-ASI06]. Controlling the AI, including sandboxing it, depends on the system's security requirements, so the guide takes the threat model next [AP].

### Preparing threat models

The guide says defining security requirements is vital: "Neither humans nor AI can determine whether something is a vulnerability without a clear definition for a specific project." [V] (Finding.md, § "Preparing threat models"). A common way to define them is a threat model, which also gives an approach to analysing and addressing the requirements; "system context" and "trust boundaries" are, for the guide's purposes, part of the threat model [AP]. It cites Adam Shostack's four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job [BT] [Shostack2014], and points readers new to threat modelling elsewhere, focusing on AI-specific issues [AP].

At least two threat models apply when AI helps develop a system [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing threat models"). The first covers the development, build, test and release environments, including the AI systems and CI/CD pipeline: an AI may do many things you do not want, so the environment must prevent the worst cases, typically the AI attacking developers' systems, exfiltrating data (including credentials and private keys), making unauthorised changes or attacking external systems, which sandboxing addresses. The second covers the deployed environment, and is the subject of the rest of the section. The guide quotes [Aniszczyk2026] that AI and external contributors do better when a project shares how it wants the software used, acceptable deployment scenarios and known problems [BT].

The guide gives three reports on why a deployed-environment threat model matters with AI [BT] (Finding.md, § "Preparing threat models"). One report says a model "performed best on systems with well-documented threat models, system design docs, requirements, and constraints. When the threat model was well-defined, the model's findings were exploitable 90 percent of the time." [V] [BT] The same report names the model's lack of a good understanding of trust boundaries as the most common cause of false positives [BT] [Yan2026]. A Mythos Preview user reported it "needs precise prompts, explicit threat models, and validation infrastructure to turn strong reasoning into reliable security outcomes" [V] [BT] [Ziegler2026]. Without enough information on the system's context and structure, AI recommendations may fail to align with requirements, including regulatory ones [BT] [Kholoosi2025].

AI can help create a threat model, but you must interact with it, review and refine its results, and "not simply take the AI-generated threat models as truth" [V] (Finding.md, § "Preparing threat models"). The guide quotes Yan's advice to bootstrap from code, docs and vulnerability history: give the model what a new security engineer would get on day one (architecture docs, wikis, entry points, git history, past vulnerabilities), ask for a threat model with system context, assets, entry points and trust boundaries, and have the model cluster past bugs and list relevant vulnerability classes; "Make sure the threat model documents what vulnerabilities you do and don’t care about, and why." [V] [BT] [Yan2026] Tools that use AI to help build a deployed-environment threat model include OpenSSF Alpha-Omega's "Threat Model Generator" (a set of agent skills) and Matt Adams's "StrideGPT" [AP].

For threat models in a world with AI, the guide lists eight considerations [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing threat models"): design for prevention and containment, limiting lateral movement if one system is taken over [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps]; strongly limit privileges; strongly control the identity of all human and non-human entities, considering continuous identification [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps]; use layered defences so attackers must surmount several mechanisms to gain top privileges [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; study past vulnerabilities for patterns that could block whole categories of attack [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; identify specifically what is trusted (admins, specific config files and so on), since "These assumptions help separate non-exploitable bugs from actual exploits." [V] [BT] [Yan2026]; keep the threat model with the code (e.g., as `THREAT_MODEL.md`) so both are updated together [BT] [Yan2026]; and implement resiliency and rapid recovery [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps].

### Preparing the sandbox

A key task when using AI agents, especially to find and fix vulnerabilities, is to put them in a sandbox that isolates them from other systems; the guide quotes Yan: "Without it, the agent may overshoot the target and do something unexpected." [V] [BT] [Yan2026] Both the infrastructure running the agents (including its operating systems) and systems external to them (the organisation's own and other people's) need protection [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox").

*Need for sandboxes* (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox" › "Need for sandboxes"). A chatbot needs no sandbox because it can only reply; an agent does [AP]. "Do not depend on text commands alone to limit an AI." [V] Commands such as "obey the law" might sometimes help, but "all inputs to an AI are simply suggestions" [V], and an AI does not always follow a given instruction. Most AIs are designed to be highly goal-driven, often interpret commands in surprising ways, and may try to break out of their environment if they believe that is the best way to proceed [BT] [OpenAI2026-07]; and since AI cannot reliably distinguish between inputs, it may execute malicious instructions in a document it reads even against your commands [AP]. Because an AI cannot be held responsible and humans always are, AI systems should be sandboxed [AR]. The guide calls the need "not hypothetical" and lists incidents [BT]: in 2026 Hugging Face was attacked by an advanced AI model [HuggingFace2026], eventually determined to be an accidental attack by an OpenAI model [Walsh2026]; Anthropic found its models "hacked into the systems of three organisations on their own, during a private security experiment." [V] [BT] [Chia2026]; Meta's AI attacked another company during testing [Pardesi2026-08-05]; and Moonshot's Kimi K3 escaped a cybersecurity testing environment developed by the UK AI Safety Institute [Reuters2026-08-07]. Some of these breakouts trace back to failures in one startup's evaluation testbed, which affected OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta and Google DeepMind [BT] [Vanian2026] [Hart2026], so not all of these companies erred independently; the guide holds that the point still stands for AI asked to perform simulated attacks [AR].

*Value of sandboxes* (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox" › "Value of sandboxes"). An AI can learn much from reading code directly but is far more effective given tools it may find useful [BT] [Zhang2024] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed), such as code search, fuzzers and static analysers; for maximum effectiveness agents need to create code, compile it, run tests and "detonate a proof of concept" [V], in a test bed representative of the real system [BT] [Yan2026]. Like humans, AIs also do better with the data most relevant to the task [AP]. Giving tools and data to an AI whose behaviour is somewhat unpredictable is a concern, and a sandbox is what lets you provide them while keeping control [AR].

*Implementing sandboxes* (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox" › "Implementing sandboxes"). Sandboxes can use virtual machines (including microVMs), containers, or applications built to constrain AI systems such as nono [AP]. Isolation should match the analysis threat model, and "A useful rule is to match isolation to capability" [V]: reading source code, modifying or building it, executing programs, fuzzing inputs, and developing or running a PoC are increasing capabilities that generally need increasingly strong controls; "a robot reading a book may only need a quiet room; a robot using power tools needs a much safer room" [V]. Containers alone are relatively weak but often fine for a discovery agent that only reads code; anything more active, and especially PoC development to validate a finding, calls for stronger protection, since a PoC is a working attack and the AI must not attack production systems or others' systems [AP]. Typically isolate with at least a VM; VMs with large attack surfaces can sometimes be broken into, and microVMs with small attack surfaces designed for security are expected to be stronger [BT] [Dinaburg2026]; for attack creation Yan advises a microVM (like Firecracker) or a full VM with egress locked down [BT] [Yan2026]. Do not leave sensitive home-directory files such as `~/.aws`, `~/.ssh` and `.env` available to the agent [BT] [Yan2026]; consider working in a subdirectory of the VM rather than a home directory, blocking home-directory access, and layering further isolation [AP].

Capabilities should have explicit execution bounds: depending on the task, limits on wall-clock time, parallelism, CPU and memory, queued or repeated actions, tool invocations, network requests, and model or monetary budget [AP] [BT] [OWASP-LLM10]. Record when a limit ends an analysis "so that resource exhaustion or a timeout is not mistaken for successful completion" [V]; such bounds reduce runaway execution, make costs more predictable, and make runs easier to interpret and reproduce [AP]. The guide quotes Yan's advice to pin image tags, commit SHAs, dependencies and build commands and to cache a local copy so builds need no network [BT] [Yan2026]. Network access is usually needed to install tools, but it may be cut before the task begins except for reaching the model; if the model runs inside the sandbox it can even be air-gapped, which the guide calls ideal [AP]. Yan's procedure: give the sandbox network access only during setup, snapshot it, remove general network access, allow only model-API traffic through a local proxy during scanning, and load the snapshot at the start of each run [BT] [Yan2026]. A team that decides not to create PoCs may need a less strong sandbox but much more time for validation [BT] [Yan2026]. Where practical, treat agents as distinct software principals rather than letting them inherit a human user's full authority, with identifiable credentials and only the tools, resources and permissions their role needs; discovery, validation, patching and reporting agents may need different authorities, and separating them improves attribution and auditability [AP] [BT] [NIST-AgentIdentity2026] [OWASP-Agentic2026]. Built-in sandboxes in harnesses such as Goose and Claude Code are worth using, but the guide suggests adding mechanisms such as a virtual machine on top [AP].

*Establish a human gate and kill switch* (Finding.md, § "Preparing the sandbox" › "Establish a human gate and kill switch"). Decide what the AI may do and set a gate where human approval is required, which must be "simple, certain, and clear to all participants" [V]. Two example gates [AP]: the AI may create local code and commits but a human must push changes externally; or the AI may push changes for external review but a human must merge into the main branch.

> "The gate must not depend on the AI (e.g., AGENTS.md or any other input command to the AI). Never give the AI a credential that would allow it to violate the gate in the first place."
> (Finding.md, § "Establish a human gate and kill switch") [V]

More generally, the guide says to separate preferences from invariants [AR]: preferences that need judgment ("Prefer the simplest implementation") belong in the AI's instructions, while invariants must always hold and should be enforced outside the AI, because "an invariant should not live inside the probabilistic system it is meant to constrain, because the model can ignore it" [V] [BT] [TesseractedLabs2026]. Many harnesses let you run code at points in the agent loop, for example to block a push to the main branch unless tests pass; the guide calls these "hooks" and recommends them for enforcing invariants, with a limit: "Hooks check what the agent asks to do or has done, not what the resulting code can reach, so hooks don’t replace a sandbox." [V] The agent must not be able to modify or bypass these controls, since "the policy should live above the thing it governs." [V] [BT] Workflows should be audited for indirect bypasses: one team found that two AI agents with repository permissions could approve each other's pull requests, silently undermining the human approval gate [BT] [TesseractedLabs2026]. Always have a kill switch to halt the AI immediately, simple and foolproof, for example powering off the virtual machine the agents run in [AP]. Fig. 9 sits here.

### Preparing AI logging

Because mechanisms may fail, or you may later need to know what happened, enable logging of AI activity in a form the AI cannot delete or modify, recording what the user requested and what the AI-enabled system did and replied, to support detection, response and recovery [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing AI logging"). Individuals often have the harness or sandbox store logs in a directory the AI cannot normally read or write; organisations may send logs to a separate system so subversion of the original cannot erase them; and logs should be protected from unauthorised viewing because they may hold sensitive data [AP]. By default Claude Code records transcripts in `~/.claude/` for 30 days, and nono logs sandbox-relevant runtime operations, tool calls, mediated decisions and capability or path access denials into a local, cryptographically verifiable session audit trail [AP]. Adjust logging early, because "you can’t retroactively change the logging configuration for past events" [V].

### Preparing the code and documentation

An AI's effectiveness depends on its input, so code and documentation prepared for analysis give much better results [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing the code and documentation"). Improve them where they lack relevant information: type declarations, inline comments, documentation and specifications, and especially "bigger picture" information explaining *why* something was done; provide links to key data or, often better, extractions of it [AP] [BT] [Wheeler2026]. The guide reports that Daniel Stenberg finds AI tools can reason across protocols, specs and third-party libraries in "almost magical ways" [V] [BT], identifying spec non-compliance and inconsistencies between comments and implementations [BT] [Vaughan-Nichols2026-02], and that language models' use of context such as comments can be powerful [BT] [Wolff2026]. At least include an `AGENTS.md` file, whose format comes from the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation; OpenAI Codex and Google Gemini supported it from the start, Claude Code historically looked only at `CLAUDE.md` but as of 2026-09-18 (version 2.1.277) reads `AGENTS.md`, and for a system that supports only another filename the guide suggests using that file to point to `AGENTS.md` so agent instructions live in one portable place [AP]. The guide quotes a seven-question documentation checklist from [0xkato2024]: up-to-date comments, third-party dependencies, a system architecture overview, mapped data flow and transaction lifecycle, clearly outlined access control, a risk assessment and threat model, and a list of known issues with explanations [BT]. AI can help write missing documentation, with review, and [Wheeler2026] advises it "work bottom-up, so that the AI can maximally build on other documentation" [V] [BT]; the guide quotes Mark Dominus that people who always wrote meticulous documentation "are now reaping new benefits from that always valuable practice" [V] [BT] [Dominus2026-03-05].

### Preparing CI/CD

Before letting AI change code, ensure a robust CI/CD system that can rigorously check its work [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing CI/CD"). The guide quotes Anthropic that an AI works best when it can check its work with a "task verifier", "a trusted method of confirming whether an AI agent’s output actually achieves its goal" [V] [BT] [Anthropic2026-03]. The guide's own addition [AR]: because task verifiers are trusted to accept or reject an agent's work, they become part of the workflow's trusted computing base, and a broken test, incomplete harness, compromised build environment, or verifier checking the wrong property "can confidently approve an incorrect result" [V]; so keep verifiers deterministic where practical, state what property each proves, and periodically test them with known-good and known-bad cases [AP]. Software that must work correctly should already have a CI/CD pipeline; the guide defines continuous integration as frequent merging and verification before acceptance, and CD as either continuous delivery or continuous deployment [AP]. A process that relies on people remembering to test, or on manual testing, cannot handle the volume of vulnerabilities and fixes today's systems require [AP]. Quality measures [AP]: a good automated test suite, with negative tests, good statement coverage (e.g., 90%-100%) and branch coverage [BT] [0xkato2024], edge-case tests [BT] [0xkato2024], and failure reports that name the failing test, expected and actual results; linters; SAST tools; and steps to minimise false positives, especially repeat ones, for example by marking confirmed false positives with suppression comments.

"Speed matters" [V] in these processes: what matters is deploying the fix before an attacker exploits it [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing CI/CD"). On CI time, the guide quotes Cloudflare: "If regression testing takes a day, you cannot get to a two-hour SLA without skipping it" [V] [BT] [Bourzikas2026]; most of the work parallelises easily, so aim for "total minutes, at worst an hour, not a day or longer for most projects" [V], acknowledging that this is hard for operational technology or software that controls physical devices while holding that the principle still applies, since "If CI takes too long, CI becomes the bottleneck." [V] It also urges speeding deployment [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps]. A CI/CD process that may take input from untrusted users must be protected, which "definitely" includes an AI agent reviewing proposals in CI/CD [AP].

### Preparing dependency updates

Modern software is mostly reused software (dependencies), in which vulnerabilities are likely to be found, especially under initial AI analysis; hunting vulnerabilities that a readily available update would resolve wastes effort [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preparing dependency updates"). Set up easily applied automated reporting of dependency vulnerabilities; many tools can raise a merge/pull request that runs the CI/CD pipeline so it can be accepted if it passes, some updates can be fully automatic, and AI can help install and configure these tools since the work is rote [AP]. It is sometimes possible to show a dependency's vulnerability is not exploitable in your system, but hard to be confident of that, so "It’s often safer and more efficient to simply update your system when a vulnerability is found in a dependency." [V] An updated dependency is fixed, and the project is better prepared for the next vulnerability in it [AP]. The guide recommends evaluating dependencies as well as first-party code, reporting what is found so dependencies can fix it for all their users, often best by partnering with the projects most important to you [AP].

## Part V: Core tasks for finding and fixing vulnerabilities
