The core tasks are identifying findings (including reports from others), deduplicating, validating, triaging, fixing, verifying fixes, reporting vulnerabilities in others' components, and releasing and deploying fixes; in practice they overlap and loop, for example deduplicating again after validation and repeating the whole process [AP] (Finding.md, § "Core tasks for finding and fixing vulnerabilities").

### Identify findings

Pointing a generic AI coding agent at an arbitrary repository and asking it to find vulnerabilities *can* work, in the sense that it may find one, especially if the software has not been examined by AI before or the model is good at program analysis [AP] [BT] [Bourzikas2026] (Finding.md, § "Identify findings"). But this trivial approach often gives little meaningful coverage of sizeable codebases and may not identify valuable findings; doing a good job generally needs a larger process around the AI to keep it focused, and many vulnerability-finding systems add one [AP] [BT] [Rogers2025]. Two reasons, especially for less-capable models [AP]: *context*, since a single agent's window fills easily and an agent often struggles with too much irrelevant information; and *throughput*, since running several agents in parallel beats one at full capacity [BT] [Bourzikas2026]. Coverage is better when "many agents work on tightly scoped questions and we deduplicate the results afterward, rather than asking one agent to be exhaustive" [V] [BT] [Bourzikas2026].

*Separate identifying findings from validation* (Finding.md, § "Identify findings" › "Separate identifying findings from validation"). The guide calls this "One excellent way to improve results" [V]: a finding is only a report that *might* be a vulnerability, because its exploitability is unclear. It cites Cloudflare that bug and reachability questions are better asked separately [BT] [Bourzikas2026], and Anthropic:

> "discovery should find as many vulnerabilities as possible—even unlikely ones—and verification should exclude findings that are not actually exploitable. When an agent tries to do both in the same step, it can self-censor and exclude exploitable true positives."
> (Finding.md, § "Separate identifying findings from validation"; the guide quoting [Yan2026]) [V] [BT]

Fig. 10 sits here.

*Helping to identify findings* (Finding.md, § "Identify findings" › "Helping to identify findings"). The guide lists eleven ways to help the AI identify findings:

1. *Give the AI tools* for searching and reading code, security tools and so on; ask the AI what tools it needs [BT] [Yan2026]; provide basics such as Python so it can write its own tools [AP].
2. *Use traditional non-AI tools* that search for potential vulnerabilities: static analysis of source or binary, and dynamic analysis including fuzzers and web application scanners [AP]. "Agentic AI is already beginning to help scale vulnerability discovery by leveraging traditional tooling" [V] [BT] [Rohlf2025]. AI agents can triage backlogs of unreviewed static analysis warnings: a 2026 study found LLM-based agents reduced an initial false-positive detection rate of over 92% on the OWASP Benchmark to as low as 6.3% in the best configuration, but that same configuration wrongly dismissed 22.25% of the real vulnerabilities, with miss rates over 50% in some categories such as weak cryptography, and the authors conclude FP suppression "should not be fully automated" [V] [BT] [Xiong2026]. "Use AI to prioritize such warnings, not to silently discard them." [V]
3. *Prioritise especially concerning code*: one list names code that parses untrusted input, enforces authentication or authorisation, or is reachable from the internet [BT] [Cycode2026, quoting Anthropic]; Firefox's scanning focuses on areas chosen "based on a mix of human judgment and automated signals." [V] [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]
4. *Search for language-specific issues, insecure coding practices, and improper handling of parameters, variables and data flows*, applying language- and framework-specific checks and tracing parameters and variables through the code [BT] [Rogers2025].
5. *Have the model examine and cluster past bugs or vulnerabilities*, list the relevant vulnerability classes, check whether each past fix was complete and applied everywhere, and look for similar problems [AP]. The guide reports Yan's account of a team that did this and found three exploitable issues in an hour: "‘What have people exploited in the past’ is sometimes a much easier cheat-code towards success than ‘find me vulnerabilities in this codebase.’" [V] [BT] [Yan2026]
6. *Use "top" lists of the most likely kinds of vulnerabilities*, at least looking for common ones, since "Most software security issues discovered each year are simply variants or instances of previously discovered patterns, rather than entirely new classes of vulnerabilities" [V] [BT] [Rohlf2025]. For a web application, the OWASP Top 10, plus relevant chapters of the OWASP ASVS as a checklist of requirements to verify [BT] [OWASP-ASVS5]; for an agentic system, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026; for anything else, including IoT, the CWE Top 25 [AP].
7. *Look for cases where one component assumes another does something but no test verifies it*; Zimmer reports that "Many vulnerabilities are being found ‘in the seams’ between programs" [V] [BT], for example a library that does not filter headers although its spec requires it and its users expect it [BT] [Zimmer2026].
8. *Examine security properties across transitions and steady-state data flows*: authentication and re-authentication, token refresh and expiry, logout and revocation, account or role changes, retries and recovery flows, and interfering concurrent operations; ask the AI to identify the invariants that should hold across transitions and look for paths that violate them [AP] [BT] [OWASP-ASVS5-V7].
9. *Include important non-security bugs*, focusing on critical issues likely to cause crashes, severe malfunction or significant instability, since important "non-security" defects can often be exploited [AP]. The guide reports Rogers's claim that "the greatest success I had with policies was a really simple policy of ‘find all bugs, even if they’re not vulnerabilities’" [V] [BT] [Rogers2025]. Cases where claimed intent (in documentation, including comments) disagrees with the code should be treated as bugs [AP].
10. *Consider disabling some production hardening mechanisms when finding and later validating*, so that hardening is truly an additional defence-in-depth measure [AP] [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; the guide takes this up again under hardening.
11. *Include information on configuration, dependencies, deployment choices and how components are combined*, since many exploitable issues emerge from these rather than as obvious defects in application source code [BT] [Ziegler2026].

Focus each analysis on specific files or functions; many practitioners first use AI to identify the most important files and functions [AP] (Finding.md, § "Helping to identify findings"). The right level of prescription is not clear at the time of writing: Yan claims that with frontier models more prescriptive prompts, such as long checklists, worsen discovery because they "tend to reduce the model’s creativity and generate fewer novel bugs" [V] [BT] [Yan2026], while others do not report the same; but "all the sources we’ve seen agree that providing a threat model and tools is vital" [V].

When requesting findings, define the output: a structured report with predefined fields ordered so the model's reasoning builds on each (rationale, finding, impact, severity and so on) [BT] [Yan2026], and very detailed information per finding, including description, filenames, line numbers, the specific triggering input and configuration, and relevant URLs [BT] [Rogers2025] (Finding.md, § "Helping to identify findings"). Ask for a PoC if the AI can provide one, but make clear findings must be reported without one, because "we don’t want to pre-filter findings too early" [V]. Where practical, include provenance: the source revision examined, environment and configuration, the analysis or verifier invocation that produced the evidence, and the threat-model assumptions used, so a result can be reproduced, rechecked after the software changes, and so a reader can "distinguish observed evidence from an AI-generated explanation" [V] [BT] [SARIF2.1].

*Managing findings* (Finding.md, § "Identify findings" › "Managing findings"). Track findings systematically, in an issue tracker or database, recording details and status, and have agents take items from the list [AP]. The guide quotes Yan that "discovery is now straightforward to parallelize, and the bottleneck has shifted to verification, triage, and patching." [V] [BT] [Yan2026] Not all findings are vulnerabilities, and counts can mislead: as one writer put it, Glasswing is reporting tens of thousands of findings, "of which a confident count of real bugs is much smaller" [V] [BT] [Ottenheimer2026-05-26]. The guide adds:

> "Repeatedly make it clear that a finding is not a confirmed vulnerability; a finding is a possible vulnerability."
> (Finding.md, § "Managing findings") [V]

Do not assume one run found everything: AI systems are non-deterministic [BT] [Rogers2025], re-running may yield more even after every earlier finding was examined, and discovering and validating vulnerabilities involves mathematically undecidable problems [BT] [Rohlf2025]; done well it should show diminishing returns, best seen by re-running until the process increasingly comes up empty [AP]. Distinguish a completed analysis with no findings from one that did not complete: a timeout, model or tool failure, environment failure, insufficient permission or policy denial "is not evidence that no vulnerabilities were found" [V], and automated workflows should record such outcomes separately so an incomplete analysis cannot silently become a "no findings" result [AP] [BT] [SARIF2.1].

### Handle external findings

"Handle external vulnerability reports as findings." [V] (Finding.md, § "Handle external findings"). Outside reports may be false, especially AI-generated ones, since AI may not understand the context [AP]. The guide names a widespread problem, "AI slop reports": AI-generated reports that are nonsense and waste everyone's time [AP]. Countermeasures it suggests [AP]: make clear that reporters should have a human review an AI-proposed report; encourage reporters to deduplicate before reporting (for example through Akrites); require evidence suggesting a vulnerability, in particular a sample input demonstrating it; and, where reporters can see the code, ask for filenames, line numbers and, if possible, a proposed fix, which even when not directly useful often clarifies what the reporter believes the problem is.

Several programmes changed policy in 2026 because of AI-generated reports, which the guide calls instructive [BT] (Finding.md, § "Handle external findings"). curl ended its bug bounty on 2026-01-31; Stenberg explained that in previous years somewhere north of 15% of submissions were confirmed vulnerabilities, but from 2025 the rate fell below 5% [BT] [Stenberg2026-01]. In March 2026 curl went back to receiving reports through HackerOne, still without bounties, and Stenberg then reported "The slop situation is not a problem anymore" [V] [BT]: reports came at about double the 2025 rate, nearly all used AI, and the confirmed rate was back to "somewhere in the 15-16% range" [V] [BT] [Stenberg2026-04]. The guide's reading: "We believe this is evidence that AI slop is a problem that can be countered." [V] HackerOne paused submissions to its Internet Bug Bounty, saying "The balance between findings and remediation capacity in open source has substantively shifted" [V] [BT] [Cooter2026]. GitHub raised its bounty requirements in May 2026 to "A working proof of concept with demonstrated security impact." [V] [BT], while welcoming AI-assisted research that is validated before submission [BT] [Brown2026]. The lesson the guide draws [AR]: publish a clear vulnerability reporting policy (e.g., in `SECURITY.md`) stating the evidence required (such as a reproducing input), that reporters must validate reports first, and that AI-assisted reports meeting those requirements are welcome; if offering rewards, watch whether they attract low-effort submissions; and for setting up a coordinated vulnerability disclosure programme, see [CISA2026-CVD].

### Deduplicate

Deduplication eliminates duplicate reports so that effort is not duplicated, since external reports and internal analysis may repeatedly identify the same problem [AP] (Finding.md, § "Deduplicate"). It has to be repeated as information arrives: before validation, to drop obvious duplicates, and again after validation [AP]. Some writers fold deduplication into triage (e.g., [Yan2026]) and others keep them separate; "No matter how you define the terms, all are needed." [V] The guide passes on Yan's recommendations [BT] [Yan2026]: consider the root cause, since scanners often flag one bug at several call sites or several symptoms of one root cause, running first a cheap deterministic pass ("same file, same category, vulnerability line numbers within ten lines of each other" [V] [BT]) and then having a model apply qualitative rules; treat as duplicates the same root cause worded differently, the same vulnerability at several call sites, a missing global protection (such as an auth check) reported per endpoint, and a cause and its consequence flagged on the same path; treat as distinct different vulnerability classes in one file, different variables reaching different sinks, two independent bugs in one helper, and the same missing check on two endpoints where each needs its own fix; and, given a PoC and candidate patch per finding, "check if the patch for one finding also disarms the PoCs of others" [V] [BT], since if it does they likely share a root cause. A finding that is not clearly a duplicate should be validated separately; more information may settle it later [AP].

### Validate findings

A vulnerability is a defect an attacker can exploit to violate a security requirement, while a finding is only a potential vulnerability, and not all findings from AIs (or humans) are real [AP] [BT] [Ottenheimer2026-05-26] (Finding.md, § "Validate findings"). So each finding must be validated to determine independently whether it is a vulnerability, a defect but not a vulnerability, or neither; a finding that is not a defect may still suggest future improvements, but the section concentrates on vulnerabilities [AP]. Fig. 11 sits here.

*Defining what a vulnerability is* (Finding.md, § "Validate findings" › "Defining what a vulnerability is"). A threat model and/or security requirements are key, since otherwise there is no way to tell whether something is security-related; a validation infrastructure, a way to run tests that confirm or refute claims, is also vital [AP] [BT] [Ziegler2026]. An important decision is whether to disable or ignore defence-in-depth countermeasures during validation, such as the software's own process sandboxing (distinct from the sandbox around the AI) [AP]. The guide's position [AR]: "A mechanism is only a defense-in-depth measure if it’s an additional security measure, not a required one." [V] So, from a security perspective, it is better to treat something as a vulnerability even if another countermeasure would have prevented it. Firefox does this, its rationale being that real-world attackers generally need to chain several exploits to escalate through layers such as sandboxing [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. Vulnerabilities that penetrate existing countermeasures should still be prioritised [AP].

*Defining the proof required* (Finding.md, § "Validate findings" › "Defining the proof required"). Projects must define the level of proof needed for a finding to count as a vulnerability [AP]. The guide's considerations [AP]: the gold standard is a PoC, a specific input an adversary could supply that makes the system fail its security requirements; in practice many projects accept triggering abnormal execution (a crash, memory error or sanitizer violation) as proof that a defect is real and reachable, and Firefox classifies findings as high-severity vulnerabilities from predictable AddressSanitizer crash symptoms such as use-after-free or out-of-bounds memory issues, its threat model assuming any could be exploitable with enough effort [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; some AI systems' guardrails prevent PoC creation, which makes them useless for that; a project may accept a more general description of how to exploit a vulnerability; and in the long term it is often worth fixing defects without a PoC, since a different AI system might find a way to exploit them, though triage usually takes known-exploitable findings first. It helps to state the evidence level explicitly; from weakest to strongest, a PoC may show that an input triggers abnormal behaviour; that the input violates a specific security property, shown by a test; that an attacker can gain a specific capability against a realistically deployed system (code execution, file read or write, authentication bypass), possibly by chaining defects; or that an attacker can do so reliably, with a working exploit [AP]. Some researchers name these levels: Antiproof distinguishes a "proof of vulnerability", "an executable test that uses a bug oracle, such as a test harness with assertions, to demonstrate a violation of a security property in isolation", from a "proof of exploitability", "an end-to-end test that demonstrates an attacker capability against a deployed system" [V] [BT] [Shakevsky2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). Firefox treats even the first level as enough to call a finding high-severity [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. Whatever level is chosen, the inverse does not hold: "failure to produce a working PoC is not proof of a false positive" [V] [BT] [Yan2026]. Validation usually includes AI review of findings; a stronger model should do better in principle but offers no guarantee [AP], and XBOW found that with Mythos Preview "judgment results were more mixed than its discovery results" [V] [BT]: it rejected false positives better than many predecessors but sometimes lost true positives when the evidence did not formally meet its criteria or the intended rule was broader than the written one [BT] [Ziegler2026].

*Tips for validation* (Finding.md, § "Validate findings" › "Tips for validation"). "There’s no magic to validation." [V] Validating claims has long been part of software development; the guide quotes a study in which practitioners emphasised a layered approach of manual inspection, sandbox testing, peer review, and cross-checking against standards such as OWASP or NIST [BT] [Kholoosi2025], and calls this part of using multiple stages to validate and deduplicate [AP] [BT] [Rogers2025]. Its tips, drawn from [Yan2026] and [Bourzikas2026] [BT]:

- The verifier should be independent of the discovery agent, because "validation involves independent reproduction rather than self-review" [V] [BT]; asking the discovery agent to reconsider its own conclusion can preserve the same context, assumptions and reasoning errors [BT].
- The verifier should try to *disprove* the finding and produce reproducible evidence. Yan's version: run the verifier in a fresh container with no shared filesystem or conversation history, since a verifier exposed to the discoverer's reasoning may simply agree, and give it only the PoC or written finding and the codebase, so it can search for mitigations the finder missed (upstream validation, auth gates, type constraints, unreachable code) [BT].
- Alternatively, give the verifier the full information but prompt it to assume each finding is a false positive and search for reasons it is wrong, with clear criteria for a true positive; this matters most when the discovery output has no PoC [BT].
- Across the teams Anthropic worked with, adding an adversarial verifier "roughly halved the rate of non-exploitable findings" [V] [BT] from discovery, and requiring that verifier to also build a PoC brought the false positive rate "to near zero" [V] [BT].
- One team scanning open source packages closed the loop by scanning a package, generating a PoC, then deploying a mock application that uses the package and triggers the PoC; their take: "Validation is the biggest holdup and the PoC is the validation." [V] [BT]

"Do not treat agreement among AI reviewers as proof." [V] In a 2026 case study of an adversarial multi-agent review process, ten dedicated AI reviewers "unanimously endorsed a non-existent Bleichenbacher padding oracle in OpenSSL's CMS module; it was killed only by a single empirical test" [V] [BT] [Agarwal2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). The guide defines empirical confirmation as actually running the target software with a test, PoC or equivalent that demonstrates the claimed failure in the target itself [AP]. The study's author concluded that "empirical verification, not consensus count, is what changes our belief" [V] [BT], added a mandatory gate ("no candidate reaches disclosure without empirical confirmation." [V] [BT]), and with it the pipeline "killed roughly 79% of 171 candidates before advancing to disclosure" [V] [BT] while still producing 4 CVEs and 8 merged security-related fixes [BT].

"PoCs must measure target behaviour, not their own artifacts." [V] A PoC's checking script can be wrong: in the same study one PoC "detected its own nonce computation rather than the library’s leak" [V] [BT], falsely confirming the vulnerability [BT] [Agarwal2026]. A PoC needs checking too, and the fix must make the PoC fail [AP]. A 2026 reproducibility study of published LLM/agent-driven vulnerability research reran the researchers' own verification checks: in 20 of 30 cases the check still reported the vulnerability on the patched version, and 7 of 19 negative controls "still trigger on benign input" [V] [BT]; as it says, "A trigger on the vulnerable build is not evidence of CVE-specific reproduction without a clean patched counterfactual." [V] [BT] [Chen2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). So, when accepting a PoC as evidence, the guide says to confirm that it triggers the specific claimed failure (not just any crash) on the vulnerable version, does not trigger on benign inputs, and does not trigger once the vulnerability is fixed [AP]. Its summary: "Ask a separate AI instance to disprove the findings, and if it can’t, demand a PoC." [V] Each step can sharply reduce false positives, and keeping them separate stops the AI abandoning findings too quickly [AP].

### Triage

Most projects must triage, that is, prioritise reports, because when there is a lot to do fixing everything immediately is impractical [AP] (Finding.md, § "Triage"). Triage is best done after validation, though an overwhelmed validation process may force some triage first [AP]. "Triage is fundamentally a risk decision." [V] Risk turns on *likelihood* (the preconditions for exploitation and what an attacker needs [BT] [Yan2026]; an unauthenticated remote exploit is more likely to be targeted than one needing a local authenticated user) and *impact* (remote code execution is typically extremely high impact; revealing only public or unimportant information is low) [AP]. Most systems have some severity rating scheme [BT] [Rogers2025]; many report that AI systems are not very good at estimating severity, rating both too high and too low, so a human should review any AI estimate that matters [AP].

AI severity estimates become more reliable when the AI is given the threat model and answers specific questions before assigning severity [AP]. The guide passes on Yan's questions about reachability, attacker control, preconditions, authentication, read versus write access and blast radius [BT], and Yan's thresholds: "zero preconditions with unauthenticated remote access is critical or high severity. One or two preconditions, or an authenticated path, is medium. Three or more, or local-only, is low. Adjust the thresholds to your system." [V] [BT] That report argues that "going through the evidence first keeps the model from anchoring on the bug class" [V] [BT] and inflating severity to match [BT] [Yan2026].

Because modern AI is increasingly good at chaining defects, something that appears unexploitable may, combined with others, become a serious vulnerability; so it is reasonable to triage the most dangerous first, but apparently unexploitable defects should not be ignored, and should be fixed as resources permit so they do not become links in a chain [AR] (Finding.md, § "Triage"). Nor should an AI-found vulnerability be assumed to stay unknown: when many people use similar tools on the same code they find the same bugs around the same time, and the Linux kernel security team reports AI-assisted findings "systematically surface simultaneously across multiple researchers, often on the same day" [V] [BT] [Linux-SecurityBugs]. Fig. 12 sits here.

### Fix vulnerabilities

"Finding vulnerabilities is useless for a defender unless those vulnerabilities are fixed." [V] (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities"). Unless fixing is efficient, the volume can become overwhelming; the guide's example is the number of Chrome bug fixes, showing a huge rise in 2026 compared with 2024–2025 caused by AI-discovered defect reports (Fig. 13) [BT] [Chrome2026]. Firefox had a similar experience: "We fixed a total of 423 security bugs in releases in April." [V] [BT], 271 announced two weeks earlier, 41 externally reported and 111 discovered internally [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. A web browser is in many ways a worst case, given its functionality and direct exposure to potentially malicious websites, but the guide takes this experience to show that AI can find many vulnerabilities not found otherwise and that teams must be ready to fix far more than before [AR].

*Fixing may be necessary for sending reports to external organizations* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "Fixing may be necessary for sending reports to external organizations"). A finder reporting to an external project, especially an open source one, may be required to propose a fix [AP]. Historically a finder might simply report and let the project fix it, but with many projects now inundated, recipients of an AI-found vulnerability often expect both a PoC and a specific proposed fix [AP]. The guide quotes Trail of Bits: "Anyone can file an issue, flex, and walk away. We showed up with the patches" [V] [BT], going beyond bug fixes to add tests, fuzzing harnesses, CI security scanning, supply-chain tooling, correctness fixes and features [BT] [TrailofBits2026-06]. A proposed fix is more likely to help than a complaint alone [AP].

*Assigning the fix* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "Assigning the fix"). A fix is developed only if someone is assigned, tacitly or explicitly; in small projects that is obvious, but in larger ones assignment itself can overwhelm [AP]. Automatic routing of an issue to the right component and human owner can help greatly [BT] [Chrome2026]; an AI system can often estimate this, and there should be a process for transferring misassigned work or an overloaded owner's work [AP].

*Creating tests and confirming the root problem* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "Creating tests and confirming the root problem"). Before fixing, create a test and confirm the root problem [AP]. The guide quotes Yan: "Write a new test that fails with the existing code." [V] [BT] Then implement the fix and confirm the same test passes without breaking anything else, which Yan calls test-driven development; without the test, the fix can silently regress and the bug can be hard to prove real [BT] [Yan2026]. The guide adds that this mistake has happened before, and a focused test makes recurrence less likely [AP]. Find the root cause: "Models may narrowly address findings at a specific call site instead of the root cause." [V] [BT] Prompting the model to identify and fix the root cause can be effective, followed by a search for variants at two levels, the same pattern elsewhere and the same class (one SQL injection suggests more), and an update of the threat model with the validated findings and patches [BT] [Yan2026].

*How to create the fix* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "How to create the fix"). AI can help develop a candidate fix, and it need not be the AI that found the vulnerability; finding models are often expensive, slow or restricted, and a different system may lack their issues, can use the detailed information gathered, and may be better at fixing [AP]. The guide names a tradeoff: the Linux kernel's procedure notes that "fixes written in the same session as used to find the bug will generally lead to better and more accurate fixes as the LLM’s reasoning context remains present" [V] [BT] [Linux-AI], but that context may include the finder's incorrect guesses; either way, give the fixing AI the verified evidence and verify the result [AP].

*Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "Only provide correct information, especially if fully automated"). Give the AI only verified correct information, especially in a fully automated process; "garbage in, garbage out" applies with particular force to AI-created fixes [AP]. Pass along what validation confirmed (such as the reproducing input), not the finder's unverified explanation of the cause or fix [AP]. The guide quotes the 1Password report: incorrect guidance in the initial prompt cut fix correctness by roughly 50 percentage points, while more correct details raised it by only 15 points over no specific guidance, so where bug details or fix guidance cannot be trusted (for example when sourced from other automated tooling), the safer bet may be to omit lower-confidence information that could cause a "correctness collapse" if wrong [BT] [Mierczuk2026].

*Approaching fixes* (Finding.md, § "Fix vulnerabilities" › "Approaching fixes"). The guide offers prompt statements for creating a fix [AP]: identify the root causes and approaches that fix them rather than only the specific example; discuss options with pros and cons; "Remember that the goal is to ensure an attacker cannot exploit the vulnerability along any path, not simply some paths." [V]; reuse existing code, minimise new code and work within the existing system; keep the change easy to review; maintain existing functionality where practical and insert no new vulnerabilities; update documentation; use tools to obtain and validate information; and pass all CI/CD tests. It quotes 1Password's advice to let the fixing AI "interrogate, validate, and raise disagreements about the information stated to them in their initial task prompts" [V] [BT] [Mierczuk2026], since an AI with wrong or missing information is much less likely to succeed [AP]. Identifying and fixing the true cause without breaking functionality is vital [AP]. The guide reports that PatchBench found the most common failure was the AI guarding the *symptom* with incomplete local checks; it also reports failures to localise the vulnerability, and broader conditions that reject benign as well as invalid input [BT] [Shen2026-09]. The guide's intervening clause about deleting the offending operation or the entire functionality is grammatically ambiguous (it is phrased as a failure "to silence the crash by deleting" them [V]), so this reference does not resolve its meaning. The guide calls the Chrome team's process instructive: a fixing agent returns several candidate fixes, a critic agent judges the best fit and produces artefacts for developers, and the two loop in a way that mimics code review [BT] [Chrome2026].

The guide warns to "be wary of long, unreviewed loops where an AI repeatedly “improves” its own code" [V]. One study ran 400 code samples through 40 rounds of AI-only improvements and found "a 37.6% increase in critical vulnerabilities after just five iterations" [V] [BT] [Shukla2025] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). A 2026 study of AI repair of Terraform infrastructure-as-code, feeding validator errors back for up to five iterations, found a previously passing security check later failed in 13.8% of scenarios; only 3.3% were unambiguous, which the authors believe is an under-count; regressions were strongly associated with large rewrites; and compliance stopped improving after about three iterations: "Three iterations capture most of the compliance improvement while keeping regression risk manageable" [V] [BT] [Agyekum2026] (listed in the bibliography for ESEM 2026). The guide's rule: "Limit the number of iterations, prefer small changes, and bring in a human when the AI doesn’t converge quickly." [V]

### Verify fixes

Candidate fixes should be reviewed first by AI and then by humans, whether a human or an AI wrote them, and especially for AI-created code [AP] (Finding.md, § "Verify fixes"). "Even very good AI writes vulnerable code." [V] An AI can be good at finding vulnerabilities and still write code full of them, because it is trained on a great deal of insecure software and it is harder to make an AI act against its training data [BT] [CSA2026] [Zimmer2026]; and because modern AI is probabilistic, its output for a request is hard to predict [BT] [Kholoosi2025].

*Have AI review the fix first* (Finding.md, § "Verify fixes" › "Have AI review the fix first"). The guide quotes Yan: "Have a new discovery agent probe the patch as an attacker to confirm the patch is comprehensive" [V] [BT] [Yan2026]. Having AI write tests for fixes helps; Chrome uses test-writing agents that make tests work across platforms and configurations before a developer reviews the fix, "saving up to weeks of developer time" [V] [BT] [Chrome2026]. Run the validated PoC against the fixed version and confirm it fails, then have a separate agent try variations of it, "since a fix that blocks only the exact PoC input isn’t a full fix" [V].

*Have humans review the fix* (Finding.md, § "Verify fixes" › "Have humans review the fix"). AI review is a good first pass, but fixes still need expert human review, because AI fixes are often incomplete, add vulnerabilities or break functionality [AP]. Three problems for reviewers to watch for [AP]:

- *AI often fixes the specific instance rather than the root cause.* The guide quotes Rogers that patches "focused too much on immediate consequences of issues" [V] [BT] and failed to put the whole application and code path into perspective [BT] [Rogers2025].
- *AI often fails to customise the fix and reuse existing constructs*, for example writing a new input-sanitising function where the developer wants to reuse an existing sanitisation library, which often prevents direct use of the fix [BT] [Steenhoek2025] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). Writing duplicate code is easier for the AI but "typically creates a maintenance nightmare" [V].
- *AI sometimes adds dependencies that do not exist, or are not the ones you think.* Attackers can register hallucinated names and wait for installs ("slopsquatting"), so any added or changed dependency should be confirmed as the real, intended and needed package [AP]. A 2025 study of 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs available in 2024 found "the average percentage of hallucinated packages is at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models" [V] [BT] [Spracklen2025] (listed in the bibliography for USENIX Security 25). A 2026 replication on five newer models found rates from 4.62% to 6.10%, with the only open-weight model analysed, DeepSeek V3.2, at 5.89% [BT] [Churilov2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed); the guide reads this as the open-weight model improving dramatically on the older average while commercial closed rates stayed about the same [AP], and quotes the author: "an order-of-magnitude compression of the inter-model spread observed by Spracklen, but not a retirement of the threat" [V] [BT]. Another 2026 study found no hallucinated package names in the imports of 1,134 short Python snippets that six models (two of them small local open-weight models) generated for everyday tasks with mainstream libraries, but when prompts asked for niche or nonexistent libraries every model imported nonexistent packages, and the samples were too small to show a zero rate even for everyday tasks [BT] [Hillah2026] (an arXiv paper per the bibliography, no venue listed). The authors expect package hallucination to keep declining but not to disappear [AP].

A wrong AI fix is not useless: one reporter found AI fixes "most useful for simply understanding what the problem actually was in the code" [V] [BT] [Rogers2025], and proposed fixes that should not be final can still guide developers to a correct solution [AP].

*Apply your usual verification processes* (Finding.md, § "Verify fixes" › "Apply your usual verification processes"). Apply all usual verification: peer review gates, CI/CD pipelines and branch protection rules, which the guide reports can help mitigate individual complacency about AI-generated security suggestions [AP] [BT] [Kholoosi2025]. Technology helps, but, as Anthropic notes, "the bottleneck in fixing bugs like these is the human capacity to triage, report, and design and deploy patches for them" [V] [BT] [Anthropic2026-05].

*Turn findings into durable checks* (Finding.md, § "Verify fixes" › "Turn findings into durable checks").

> "AI analysis is non-deterministic; don’t depend on rerunning it to catch the same problem again. Instead, turn what you learned into deterministic checks that run on every change, as part of the change."
> (Finding.md, § "Turn findings into durable checks") [V]

At least add the regression test created earlier; optionally also a static analysis rule for the vulnerable pattern (e.g., a Semgrep rule or CodeQL query), a fuzz harness for code that fuzzing handles well (e.g., parsers), and a hardening or API change that makes the whole vulnerability class impossible or unlikely [AP]. AI can often help build all of these [AP]. The general principle: "if something is important, enforce it with deterministic mechanisms instead of relying on an AI to notice it every time" [V].

### Report vulnerabilities

The guide covers three kinds of reporting: to a component's maintainers, to authorities where law requires it, and to your own users [AP] (Finding.md, § "Report vulnerabilities").

*Reporting to externally maintained projects* (Finding.md, § "Report vulnerabilities" › "Reporting to externally maintained projects"). Report a vulnerability in an externally maintained component to the project that maintains it, using its reporting process and preferred form, often through coordinated vulnerability disclosure [AP]. First, prevent AI slop; the guide quotes Mozilla: "AI-assisted bug reports have a mixed track record, and skepticism is earned." [V] [BT] [Grinstead2026-03] The best AI systems have improved and some apply human review before sending, but many projects still receive much useless slop [AP]. Early on, read the project's threat model and reporting guidance (e.g., `SECURITY.md`), and have any AI you use read them before drafting; the Linux kernel project specifically recommends telling the AI to do this [AP] [BT] [Linux-SecurityBugs]. Provide value: the reproducing inputs that demonstrate the vulnerability, test cases for easy verification and regression testing, and a proposed fix, all reviewed by a human before submission [AP].

The guide ties this to the human gate [AR]: treat high-impact or externally visible actions (submitting reports, publishing, merging, deploying fixes, modifying production, accessing especially sensitive resources) as explicit approval boundaries that may need separate authorisation, and where approval is required, "enforce it in the tool or workflow rather than relying only on an instruction in the AI prompt" [V] [BT] [OWASP-LLM06]. State the assumed deployment model and security threat briefly and early in the report: when AI writes the report, often neither the code nor the documentation tells it which deployments are supported, and "Many AIs will make the most permissive assumption, even a patently absurd one" [V], making any finding look especially severe; once stated, a maintainer who disagrees can correct that line rather than reject the report unexplained [AP]. Before reporting, check that the problem still exists in the current code; the Linux kernel security team says "A significant part of reports are for bugs that have already been fixed" [V] [BT], asks reporters to verify on recent versions and to identify the affected version with a stable identifier such as a commit ID or exact version rather than "latest", and to "stick to verifiable facts" [V] [BT] rather than speculative implications [BT] [Linux-SecurityBugs].

When a component's maintainers expressly do not support the reporter's threat model, the reporter can try to convince them to expand it (typically by providing resources such as proposed changes or joining as a co-maintainer); fix it and submit it as a normal non-security defect in the short term while changing their own design so it no longer needs a security property the component does not support; or use a different or additional component for that functionality [AP]. The guide's example [AE]: the Linux kernel threat model (2026) says mounting a block device is a privileged operation and the administrator is responsible for the media they mount; ChromeOS uses the Linux kernel but supports mounting an external USB stick that is not fully trusted (presumed passive), which the kernel does not support, so when ChromeOS mounts untrusted external media it uses a different system based on Filesystem in Userspace (FUSE) rather than relying solely on the kernel's built-in mechanisms. The guide's reading is that ChromeOS's developers chose components carefully, and that many problems need several components working together [AR].

Follow the project's rules for AI-assisted contributions, which more projects now have [AP]. The guide holds up the Linux kernel's rules [BT] [Linux-AI]: "AI agents MUST NOT add Signed-off-by tags." [V] [BT], since only humans can legally certify the Developer Certificate of Origin; the human submitter must review all AI-generated code, take full responsibility, and credit the AI with an "Assisted-by:" tag; the procedure requires trying to create a reproducer for any nontrivial bug, writing and testing a fix ("This part is not optional" [V] [BT]), and saying explicitly what could not be built, tested or reproduced; and the assistant "must never send anything itself" [V] [BT], since a human decides. Do not propose a fix if a project asks you not to, though most projects do want good ones [AP]. Often a project will not accept a proposed fix directly [BT] [Zimmer2026]: outside fixes often fail to reuse a project's existing methods and templates, creating maintenance issues if accepted as-is, maintainers have roadmaps a fix may not meet, and projects have unwritten rules; but a proposed fix is often a necessary and useful draft toward the final one [AP]. On report size, maintainers want something they can read quickly yet detailed enough to help; one solution is to lead with the report's essence in a single paragraph of six sentences or fewer, to find out and follow the project's preferred format, and to respect maintainers' limited time [AP] [BT] [Larson2026]. Many open source projects receive an overwhelming number of duplicate reports [BT] [PSF2026], often because many people point the same AI system at the same software; the guide quotes Linus Torvalds that "if you found a bug using AI tools, the chances are somebody else found it too" [V] [BT], and his advice to "read the documentation, create a patch too" [V] [BT] [Zorz2026]. The Linux Foundation's Akrites project helps organisations deduplicate findings before they are submitted to open source projects, and validate, prepare remediations and synchronise disclosure [AP].

*Reporting to authorities* (Finding.md, § "Report vulnerabilities" › "Reporting to authorities"). Some laws require reporting to authorities; the guide's widely applicable example is the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), which places requirements on manufacturers of products with digital elements distributed in the EU and on open source software stewards [AP]. The CRA treats *actively exploited vulnerabilities* differently: for an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident in software one maintains, strict reporting requirements have applied to manufacturers since 2026-09-11, with an initial report due within 24 hours [AP]. The CRA does not require software to have no unknown vulnerabilities, but its Annex I requires, among other things, that products "be made available on the market without known exploitable vulnerabilities" [V] [BT], with a secure-by-default configuration in general and security updates, and that manufacturers identify and document vulnerabilities and components, "address and remediate vulnerabilities without delay" [V] [BT], and apply effective and regular security tests and reviews [BT] [CRA-AnnexI]. The guide points to its course on the CRA (LFEL1001) [AP].

*Reporting to users* (Finding.md, § "Report vulnerabilities" › "Reporting to users"). Usually do not tell users about a vulnerability before a fix exists, since early announcement mainly helps attackers; coordinated vulnerability disclosure keeps a vulnerability private until a fix is ready [AP]. If users must be told earlier (for example because the vulnerability is public or actively exploited), say which versions are affected, how users can reduce risk until a fix (a workaround or configuration change) and when a fix is expected, without details that help attackers; for an actively exploited vulnerability, the CRA may require manufacturers to inform affected users [AP].

### Release and deploy

"Software that is only fixed on a developer’s workstation helps no one else." [V] (Finding.md, § "Release and deploy"). Fixed software must be released and deployed, which matters even more now that AI is accelerating vulnerability-finding [AP]. The guide quotes Anthropic that developers should make security fixes available as quickly as possible, make updates as easy as possible to install, and be more persistent with users still running vulnerable software [BT] [Anthropic2026-05]; it adds that release processes should be streamlined, updates automatically checked for a valid digital signature, and the update process kept from becoming a vulnerability itself [AP].

"A released fix is also a map to the vulnerability." [V] Attackers can patch-diff the fixed code against the previous version to work out the vulnerability, and AI has made this fast and cheap [AP]. The guide reports a June 2026 study in which Claude Mythos Preview built 8 working code-execution exploits from 18 recent Firefox security patches, writing "its first working exploit in just under one hour" [V] [BT], and produced 8 full privilege-escalation exploit chains from 21 Windows kernel vulnerabilities [BT]. Its authors warned that "A lone operator can now turn a month’s worth of patches into working exploits in a single afternoon—for a few thousand dollars and with no specialized expertise" [V] [BT], and concluded that "the typical patching playbook that software developers use today" … "no longer holds" [V] [BT] [Xiao2026]. The guide's practical conclusions [AP]: minimise the time between a fix becoming public and its release, developing security fixes privately where practical (in a private fork or private security advisory) and publishing fix, release and advisory together; release fixes for all supported versions at once, since fixing the main branch first shows attackers how to attack the long-term-support branch; shorten the security release cycle, as Mozilla moved its dot releases from monthly to roughly weekly [BT] [Xiao2026]; and make updating easy and fast. "Faster patching alone does not solve this problem." [V] The guide quotes the Xiao study: "A more durable fix would attack the supply of bugs, rather than the speed of patching them." [V] [BT], starting with migrating critical components to memory-safe languages such as Rust or hardening them with mitigations that retire whole exploit classes [BT] [Xiao2026].

When releasing a fix, tell users with a security advisory stating the vulnerability, affected versions, fixing version and what to do, and where appropriate obtain a CVE identifier so tools can alert users [AP] (Finding.md, § "Release and deploy"). Advisory writing can bottleneck when fixes arrive quickly; consider using AI to draft release notes, advisories and CVE descriptions from the fixes, with human review and repair before publication, as the Chrome team is working to automate [AP] [BT] [Chrome2026]. People, projects and organisations should also be able to *accept* updates rapidly, with automated testing that proposes or applies them; manual-only processes often cannot keep up, and "Humans still need to be in control, but the humans need to be supported by automated processes" [V] that help them notice problems and decide well [AP].

### Repeated application

AI should in most cases be applied repeatedly: most AI systems are non-deterministic, so rerunning the same system on the same inputs can find new vulnerabilities, especially in the first few iterations, and improving systems may find new problems [AP] (Finding.md, § "Repeated application"). As vulnerabilities are found, search for similar patterns and make sure the problem was fixed systematically [AP]. The guide's encouragement [AR]: improved hardening and fixing will eventually eliminate the "easy vulnerabilities" and make the system increasingly hard to attack; "Software is finite, and so are defects." [V]; and "as it gets harder for software developers to find vulnerabilities, it also gets harder for attackers to find them" [V]. Because software changes, deterministic checks (including those made from earlier findings) should run on every change, and an AI system should also analyse each proposed pull or merge request before it is accepted [AP]. Fig. 14 sits here.

## Part VI: Preventing vulnerabilities longer term

"Finding and fixing specific vulnerabilities isn’t enough." [V] Systematic prevention is also needed; the guide likens finding and quickly fixing vulnerabilities to stopping the bleeding of a badly hurt patient, important but not sufficient, and notes AI can help with prevention too [AP] (Finding.md, § "Preventing vulnerabilities longer term").

### Limit vibe coding

The guide defines *vibe coding* as using AI to generate code without a human reviewing the results, and says not to do it where the results matter for security [AP] (Finding.md, § "Limit vibe coding"). AI has become far better at generating code but often generates insecure code; where code cannot have a security impact (e.g., it does not process untrusted input), vibe coding may be fine, but where failures may cause serious problems, AI-generated code should not be accepted without review [AP]. The guide reports an explosion in vulnerable code releases from vibe coding in security-relevant code, quoting [Holterhoff2026] that researchers at Georgia Tech's Vibe Security Radar found CVEs directly attributable to AI coding tools in March 2026 alone exceeded all of 2025 combined [BT]. It urges skepticism, reporting a controlled study in which participants with an AI assistant "wrote significantly less secure code than those without access" [V] [BT] yet "were more likely to believe they wrote secure code" [V] [BT], while those who trusted the AI less and worked more on their prompts produced fewer vulnerabilities [BT] [Perry2023] (listed in the bibliography for CCS ’23). Security-focused instructions can reduce what AI code assistants get wrong in the first place, per the OpenSSF "Security-Focused Guide for AI Code Assistant Instructions" [AP] [BT] [OpenSSF2025-AIInstructions]. Where security matters, have AI look for vulnerabilities and have humans review AI-generated code [AP]. Generating code with AI can save time, especially code that handles no untrusted input and needs no particular performance; the problem lies in believing AI-generated code never has defects or vulnerabilities [AP]. Review may someday be unnecessary or fully automatable, but the authors cannot predict how good AI will get or how fast [AP].

### Evaluate merge/pull requests

In all cases, whether a change came from AI or humans, look for vulnerabilities in each merge/pull request [AP] (Finding.md, § "Evaluate merge/pull requests"). The guide's tips [AP]: have AI and a human review a change before it is even submitted; use tools that scan and report on pull/merge requests, some specialised, such as Sashiko for the Linux kernel; and, quoting the CSA, "All code (human or AI-generated) should pass LLM-driven security review before merge." [V] [BT] [CSA2026]

Running AI agents in CI/CD on proposed changes needs care: from an untrusted contributor, the title, description, comments, commit messages and code are all attacker-controlled, and an agent treats all of it as input that an attacker can use for prompt injection [AP] (Finding.md, § "Evaluate merge/pull requests"). The guide calls this "not hypothetical" and reports three cases [BT]. In 2025 Aikido Security reported "PromptPwnd", in which GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD workflows embedded untrusted issue, pull request or commit content into AI agent prompts, stating that "At least 5 Fortune 500 companies are impacted" [V] [BT] [Daelman2025]. In 2026 Aonan Guan and colleagues showed that a malicious pull request title, issue comment or hidden HTML comment could make Anthropic's Claude Code Security Review, Google's Gemini CLI Action and GitHub's Copilot Agent leak the repository's own API keys and access tokens, one of them being a security review tool; Guan's explanation is that the agents get powerful tools and secrets "in the same runtime that processes untrusted user input" [V] [BT] [Guan2026]. In the 2025 "s1ngularity" attack, compromised versions of the Nx build package ran any installed Claude, Gemini or Amazon Q command-line agent with permission checks disabled and used it to search the developer's system for secrets, which StepSecurity called "the first known case where attackers have turned developer AI assistants into tools for supply chain exploitation" [V] [BT] [Kurmi2025]. For an agent run on untrusted proposed changes, the guide's five rules [AP]: give it no secrets or write-capable tokens (GitHub Actions withholds secrets from fork pull requests by default, but some workflows grant them anyway, e.g., via the `pull_request_target` trigger, and the guide says not to do that for AI agents [BT] [Guan2026]); give a review agent the fewest tools practical, since a reviewer usually needs only to read code and report [BT] [Daelman2025], unlike an agent hunting vulnerabilities; use short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials where any are needed; treat the agent's output as untrusted data and put a human gate before any privileged action; and separate analysis from action, so a low-privilege agent reports and a different, trusted process or a human decides. Fig. 15 sits here.

### Apply secure by design and secure by default

"Only trying to find and fix software vulnerabilities one at a time will not succeed in the long term." [V] It is necessary, but future changes may reintroduce vulnerabilities, so the guide also applies the principles of secure-by-design and secure-by-default [AR] (Finding.md, § "Apply secure by design and secure by default"). *Secure-by-design* means designing software to be secure from the outset: for example, limiting attack surface and applying defence in depth [BT] [FiveEyes2026], and running security checks where attackers cannot bypass them (on the server, not only the client, if an attacker can control a client), with OWASP ASVS 5.0 requirements V2.2.2 and V8.3.1 cited on input validation and authorisation [AP] [BT] [OWASP-ASVS5]. *Secure-by-default* means releasing software secure by default at installation: "Most users install the unchanged default, so the default security is the security of most installations." [V] A post-installation "hardening guide" signals insecure defaults whose steps should have been applied before release; if needed, provide instead a "loosening guide" explaining how to disable security mechanisms in special cases and the risks [AP]. The guide quotes the Five Eyes agencies that secure-by-design and secure-by-default "must become standard practice – not an aspiration" [V] [BT] [FiveEyes2026].

### Harden

The guide defines hardening, a key aspect of secure-by-design, as "modifying the system/software so that defects are systematically unlikely to be exploitable or have more limited impact" [V], and urges applying it as much as practical (Finding.md, § "Harden"). "Defects are inevitable, but they do not necessarily need to be vulnerabilities." [V] The goal is to make defects hard to exploit and constrain their likelihood and impact [AP]. Fig. 16 sits here.

*Applying hardening* (Finding.md, § "Harden" › "Applying hardening"). Use as many hardening techniques as make sense [AP]. Some are industry-wide. Memory-unsafe languages, primarily C and C++, do not by default protect against common memory errors such as out-of-bounds reads and writes, so humans and AI alike produce more vulnerabilities in them, and they are harder to analyse, giving more false positives [AP] [BT] [Bourzikas2026]. Two approaches [AP]: rewrite in a memory-safe language such as Rust, disabling selected memory checks only where unnecessary and performance-critical; or add mechanisms that make an undetected memory-safety issue less likely to become a vulnerability, such as the OpenSSF Compiler Options Hardening Guide for C and C++ [BT] [OpenSSF2026-06], or new APIs like the Linux kernel's `strscpy`. Other hardening is program-specific, developed from lessons in that software; Mozilla, after several sandbox escapes via prototype pollution in the privileged parent process, made an architectural change to freeze those prototypes by default rather than fixing them one by one, and later saw in harness logs many attempts along that line thwarted by the design [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. "Hardening works." [V] Many well-run projects report that hardening counters attackers, including powerful AI models: Mozilla reported that "just as interesting as what the models found is what they didn’t find" [V] [BT], because the models could not circumvent Firefox's layered defences [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]; and Anthropic reported that Mythos Preview found many apparent vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel but, because of its defence-in-depth measures, "was unable to successfully exploit any of these" [V] [BT] [Carlini2026].

*Harden to counter chaining* (Finding.md, § "Harden" › "Harden to counter chaining"). Hardening has always been good practice, but AI makes it more important because hardening can sometimes counter chaining, the combination of several defects into an exploitable vulnerability; skilled humans have long done this, but AI makes chained attacks much cheaper and easier [AP]. The guide distinguishes *reliable* hardening, which consistently prevents certain kinds of defects from becoming vulnerabilities, from *unreliable* hardening, which only makes exploitation somewhat more difficult and can be circumvented with extra, typically tedious, effort [AP]. Both counter attackers without AI, and a human may judge the second kind not worth the effort, but AI sharply reduces the effort certain attacks need [AR]. The guide quotes Anthropic: "We have nearly a dozen examples of Mythos Preview successfully chaining together two, three, and sometimes four vulnerabilities in order to construct a functional exploit on the Linux kernel" [V] [BT], and "Mitigations whose security value comes primarily from friction rather than hard barriers… become considerably weaker against model-assisted adversaries" [V] [BT] [Carlini2026]. So use reliable measures [AR]: W^X ensures memory regions are writable or executable but not both, systematically preventing unauthorised memory writes from becoming directly executable; parameterised statements reliably counter SQL injection [AP]. Unreliable measures are much weaker against AI [AR]; the guide's example, quoted from Anthropic, is JIT compilation in browsers, whose dynamic, unpredictable memory layout made exploitation harder for humans, yet Mythos Preview autonomously found the needed read and write primitives and chained them into a JIT heap spray [BT] [Carlini2026]. Those layout variations were not designed to counter attacks but historically protected systems because countering them was too much effort for most human attackers, whereas an AI can determine the layout cheaply enough to make such attacks practical [AR]. ASLR illustrates the difference [AR]: it is reliable only if there are enough randomisation bits to make brute force impractical and no way for an attacker to reveal data that speeds the attack; attackers can often obtain the random value, after which AI can again chain attacks; so the guide recommends continuing to use ASLR, an easily enabled defence, but says "don’t count on ASLR alone as a defense" [V]. "Hardening still matters, but you need to use reliable hardening mechanisms." [V]

*Evaluate with hardening disabled and evaluate the hardening* (Finding.md, § "Harden" › "Evaluate with hardening disabled and evaluate the hardening"). Where sensible, disable a system's hardening when looking for vulnerabilities, to implement defence in depth [AP]. The system should, where practical, make an attacker defeat several mechanisms, and an AI evaluating only the fully hardened system will often fail to report cases where a single mechanism alone stopped an attack [AR]. In one analysis of Firefox, the testing environment "intentionally removed some of the security features found in modern browsers" [V] [BT], most importantly the sandbox [BT] [Anthropic2026-03], and in this weakened environment the AI "is tasked with developing an exploit" [V] [BT] [Anthropic2026-04s]. Also have the AI look for defects in the hardening itself, such as a sandbox escape, to check the mechanism works against active attacks; in Firefox's case the AI was "permitted to patch the Firefox source code, so long as the modified code is restricted to run only in the sandboxed process" [V] [BT], and Mozilla notes such bugs are notoriously hard to find with fuzzing [BT] [Grinstead2026-05]. Evaluating the system without its hardening, and the hardening separately, improves both and yields stronger defence in depth, where attackers often must break several mechanisms [AR].

*Harden the deployed environment and infrastructure* (Finding.md, § "Harden" › "Harden the deployed environment and infrastructure"). Organisations need to focus on security basics and harden their environment and infrastructure; what they must do is not new but now urgent [AP]. The guide quotes five actions from several government agencies [BT] [FiveEyes2026]: reduce the attack surface; accelerate patching, since AI is shortening the time between discovery and exploitation; address legacy systems, since unsupported systems "are not just technical debt; they are strategic liabilities" [V] [BT]; review and strengthen identity and access controls; and prepare for incidents before they happen. The UK NCSC recommends an "update by default" policy of applying updates as soon as possible, ideally automatically, and where not everything can be updated, prioritising external attack surfaces [BT] [Whitehouse2026]. The guide grants that updating by default is a risk (an update may break functionality, or an attacker may subvert it) but says "the risk from failing to update is usually far greater" [V]. It quotes the CSA that the basics still matter (segmentation, egress filtering, multifactor authentication, defence in depth and breadth), that egress filtering "blocked every public Log4j exploit" [V] [BT], and that "Every boundary increases attacker cost" [V] [BT], and adds the CSA's note that minimising base operating system images, or replacing third-party libraries with framework primitives, can reduce attack surface, with AI's help [BT] [CSA2026]. Many recommendations focus on identity; CrowdStrike says attacks become dangerous when they let an adversary assume a trusted identity, obtain credentials or abuse excessive privileges, and that prevention includes zero standing privileges, continuous access verification and limited credential exposure [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps]. Attackers may still get in, so logging and internal telemetry, offline backups and a Continuity of Operations Plan (COOP) remain vital [AP]. "Resilience is no longer optional" [V]: CrowdStrike says that in a frontier AI threat model, "resiliency is no longer a differentiator layered on top of prevention. It is part of prevention." [V] [BT] All this requires continuously testing security assumptions, since "Controls that look strong on paper may fail in practice." [V] [BT] [CrowdStrike2026-FiveSteps]

The guide closes the section against panic [AR]: all of this was true before AI and now simply matters more to execute, and "even the most advanced AI models cannot simply create vulnerabilities where none exist" [V]. It quotes Red Hat's Gunnar Hellekson that "context renders many bugs useless" [V] [BT], some AI-identified "vulnerabilities" being functionality bugs with no meaningful exploit path [BT] [Hellekson2026]. AI may find many "vulnerabilities" as some document defines them, many of which will not matter in a given context: "Act promptly on the ones that are." [V] (Finding.md, § "Harden the deployed environment and infrastructure")

## Part VII: Call to action, acknowledgements, bibliography and licence

*Call to action* (Finding.md, § "Call to action").

> "This doesn’t mean it’s time to panic. It means it’s time to work. Now."
> (Finding.md, § "Call to action") [V]

AI can help find and fix vulnerabilities and, over time, help developers build software with so few vulnerabilities that it will be incredibly hard to subvert; developers and those who work with them have an opportunity to make the world much more secure [AP]. The guide's four closing steps [AP]: pick your most important project and, once it is in good shape, the next; prepare (the AI, its sandbox and logging, and the software's threat model, code and documentation, CI/CD and dependency updates); find and fix vulnerabilities using AI, repeatedly, since one or a few runs can miss important vulnerabilities; and prevent longer-term problems through process improvements (such as evaluating every merge/pull request) and hardening of systems and the wider environment.

*Acknowledgements* (Finding.md, § "Acknowledgements"). The guide thanks all contributors and reviewers, including Georg Kunz, Laura Guazzelli, Ryan Jennings and Santosh Kumar Puppala [AP].

*Bibliography* (Finding.md, § "Bibliography"). 141 keyed entries: vendor and AI-lab blogs and reports, news articles, government and agency statements, standards and project documentation, papers (many listed by arXiv link only, some with conference venues), a book ([Shostack2014], with no link), and a private interview of Derek Zimmer by David A. Wheeler ([Zimmer2026], with no link) [AP]. Nineteen keys are not cited by key in the body: Ahmad2026, Anthropic-07-27, Berkeley, Buttell2026, CloudFlare, Dominus2026-03-09, Donnelly2026, Google-CodeMender-Docs, Harzevili2024, Microsoft2026-07, OWASP2025-AITesting, OWASP-GenAI, Safdar2025, Shimmi2025, Shein2026, Silverman2024, vanZyl, Veracode and Wheeler2025 (the body names the LFEL1012 course that Wheeler2025 lists, by title and URL rather than key) [AP].

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Ignoring or refusing AI, including banning AI-assisted reports.* Acceptable only where a project's sole aim is to show what humans can do without AI; otherwise "extremely harmful", and the guide's conclusion is that it can end only in compromise (Finding.md, § "Do not ignore AI").
- *Waiting for the best, restricted models before starting.* "Do not wait"; start with reasonably good, widely available models, while using advanced ones when available (Finding.md, § "Do not wait for access to the best AI models").
- *Presuming AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities.* Framed as a presumption to drop, bounded by the guide's statement that AI can help with many fixes and that its evidence is as of 2026 (Finding.md, § "Do not presume AI can correctly fix all vulnerabilities").
- *Manual, slow and closed approaches, including relying on hidden source code.* Described as failing now, with "Hiding source code doesn’t help" as a heading claim (Finding.md, § "Manual closed approaches are failing").
- *Limiting an AI by text instructions alone, or placing a gate or invariant inside the AI.* "Do not depend on text commands alone"; the gate "must not depend on the AI"; invariants belong outside the probabilistic system (Finding.md, § "Need for sandboxes"; § "Establish a human gate and kill switch").
- *Treating self-review or AI consensus as validation.* Validation is independent reproduction rather than self-review, and agreement among AI reviewers is not proof (Finding.md, § "Tips for validation").
- *Using AI to silently discard static-analysis warnings*, or letting an incomplete analysis count as "no findings" (Finding.md, § "Helping to identify findings"; § "Managing findings").
- *Long, unreviewed AI self-improvement loops on fixes.* The guide says to be wary of them, limit iterations and bring in a human (Finding.md, § "Approaching fixes").
- *Relying on reruns of AI to catch a known problem again*, rather than deterministic checks (Finding.md, § "Turn findings into durable checks").
- *Vibe coding where security matters.* Bounded: it "may be fine" for code that cannot have a security impact (Finding.md, § "Limit vibe coding").
- *Giving agents that review untrusted changes secrets, write-capable tokens or broad tools* (Finding.md, § "Evaluate merge/pull requests").
- *Fixing vulnerabilities only one at a time*, without secure-by-design and secure-by-default (Finding.md, § "Apply secure by design and secure by default").
- *Relying on unreliable, friction-based hardening, or on ASLR alone* (Finding.md, § "Harden to counter chaining").
- *Faster patching as a sufficient answer*, and the typical monthly, staged patching playbook, which the guide reports [Xiao2026] as no longer holding (Finding.md, § "Release and deploy").
- *Panic.* "This doesn’t mean it’s time to panic"; the guide's answer is work (Finding.md, § "Harden the deployed environment and infrastructure"; § "Call to action").

- **Source and conversion.** Per the acquisition manifest, the tape is the repository's Markdown at the pinned commit, concatenated with front matter and MDX imports dropped and the text otherwise byte for byte. It holds one file, `docs/Finding-and-Fixing-Vulnerabilities-Using-AI/Finding.md` (manifest: 36,745 words); the tape is 2,060 lines and 36,749 words. The operator's brief and the manifest describe Finding.md as the guide's single source file, from which the site's HTML pages are generated (the tape carries a comment that each chapter is its own H1, with "see gen-html"), and the manifest records coverage as complete; this reference carries no `coverage:` field.
- **Read coverage.** The producing session read every line of the tape (1–2,060) in bounded ranges before writing, including all 46 quiz blocks, the bibliography and the licence. Ranges are recorded in the producer receipt.
- **Citation style.** No page anchors exist; citations use the guide's headings, which are unique within this commit. Numbers given to chapters and figures are this reference's, not the guide's.
- **Quotation and markers.** `[V]` marks words found verbatim in the tape. Where those words are a third party's as quoted by the guide (vendor blogs, news, papers, agency statements), the sentence names the guide's citation key and adds `[BT]`; this reference describes the guide's report of those findings, not the cited works, which were not read. Passages the guide quotes with its own bracketed insertions are paraphrased rather than quoted. Papers the bibliography lists by arXiv link with no venue are labelled as such; venues are given where the bibliography lists one.

The eight linked videos are hosted outside the repository and are not part of the tape.
